definition: The sharp, vinegar-like acid in sourdough, made by some of the bacteria in a starter. It gives a stronger, tangier bite than lactic acid. Cooler, stiffer fermentation tends to favor acetic acid, so a stiff starter or a long cold retard usually makes a more noticeably sour loaf.
shortDefinition: The sharp, vinegar-like acid in sourdough.
henrysTips: Want a more sour loaf? Try a stiffer levain and a longer rest in the fridge. Small changes in temperature and hydration move the flavor more than you'd expect.
alternateQuestions: how to make sourdough more sour
youtubeQuery: how to make sourdough more sour

definition: A form of commercial yeast with larger granules that needs to be dissolved in warm water (bloomed) before use. It's less potent than instant yeast, so use about 25% more if you're substituting it for instant.
shortDefinition: Traditional dry yeast that needs to bloom in water.
henrysTips: If the water is too hot (over 110°F), you'll kill the yeast. Too cold, and it won't activate. Aim for 100-105°F.
youtubeQuery: active dry yeast vs instant yeast

definition: Flour that's been allowed to rest after milling so it can oxidize, which tends to make dough stronger and more predictable. Mills once aged flour for weeks, and today oxidizing agents like ascorbic acid are often used to get a similar effect. Fresh-milled flour can behave differently in its first days, and some bakers find it slacker, but many home bakers use it right away and adjust hydration and handling.
shortDefinition: Flour rested after milling so it oxidizes and strengthens.
henrysTips: I mill and bake the same day most of the time. If the dough feels a little loose, I add an extra set of folds rather than waiting on the flour.
alternateQuestions: should I age fresh milled flour

definition: A thin layer of cells between the bran and the starchy endosperm. Botanically it belongs to the endosperm, but in milling it comes off with the bran. It's rich in protein, minerals, and enzymes, so a lot of whole-grain flavor and enzyme activity is lost when it's sifted out.
shortDefinition: Nutrient-rich layer under the bran, removed with it in milling.
henrysTips: This is part of why a light sift beats a heavy one for flavor. Pull out only the coarsest bran and you keep more of what's just underneath.

definition: A small, straight-sided jar or container holding a sample of your dough, taken right after mixing, so you can track how much the dough has risen during bulk fermentation. Because it's easy to see the level in a straight-sided container, it gives you a clear read on percentage rise that's hard to judge in a big bowl. It's most useful alongside the look and feel of the main dough.
shortDefinition: A small sample jar used to track dough rise.
henrysTips: Mark the starting level with tape or a marker, and keep the jar right next to the main dough so they're at the same temperature.

definition: A medium-protein flour designed to do everything reasonably well. While it can make bread, it produces a softer, less chewy loaf than bread flour.

A tiny seed from a broadleaf plant, not a grass, so it's a pseudocereal. It was an important crop in Mesoamerica and the Andes long before European contact. Amaranth is gluten-free, with an earthy, slightly grassy flavor. Bakers use the flour in small amounts or in gluten-free blends, and the whole seeds can be popped or cooked and added to bread.
shortDefinition: Tiny gluten-free seed used like a grain.

definition: An enzyme naturally present in flour (and saliva!) that breaks down complex starches into simple sugars. Yeast then eats these sugars to produce carbon dioxide.
shortDefinition: The enzyme that turns starch into sugar for the yeast to eat.

definition: A culinary and marketing term for grains that have changed little through modern plant breeding, like einkorn, emmer, spelt, khorasan, teff, millet, and sorghum. There's no fixed scientific definition, so which grains make the list depends on who's using the label. Ancient doesn't mean gluten-free: the ancient wheats all contain gluten, and they usually ferment, absorb water, and build structure differently from modern bread wheat.
shortDefinition: Loose term for grains little changed by modern breeding.
henrysTips: Don't swap an ancient wheat into your favorite recipe one for one and expect the same loaf. Start with 20 to 30 percent of the flour, learn how it feels, then push further.

definition: Also known as Vitamin C, this is often added to bread recipes in tiny amounts to strengthen the gluten network and help the dough hold its shape during a long rise.
A measure of how much mineral content remains in flour after milling. High ash content (like in whole wheat or Type 85 flour) means more bran/germ, darker color, and higher enzyme activity.

A resting period where flour and water are mixed and left to sit (typically 30 minutes to 2 hours) before adding salt and starter/yeast. During this time, enzymes naturally present in the flour begin breaking down proteins and starches, making the dough easier to work with and improving gluten development.
shortDefinition: Resting period for flour and water before adding other ingredients.
henrysTips: This is one of the easiest ways to improve your bread without extra work. Just mix flour and water, walk away, come back later. The dough practically kneads itself.

definition: A sweet, braided bread originating from Jewish communities in Poland and Ukraine. The dough is rolled out, spread with filling (chocolate or cinnamon), rolled into a log, cut, and twisted before baking.
A ring-shaped bread that is boiled in water (often with malt or honey) before baking. The boiling step gelatinizes the crust starch, giving bagels their signature shine and chew.
A long, thin loaf of French bread characterized by a crisp crust and large, irregular holes in the crumb. It requires careful shaping and handling to preserve the air bubbles.
A heavy linen cloth used to support dough (like baguettes) while they proof. The fabric is folded up between loaves to help them hold their shape and prevent them from sticking to each other.
henrysTips: Never wash your couche! Just scrape off the flour and let it dry. It gets better with age.

definition: A system where all ingredients are expressed as a percentage of the flour weight. Flour is always 100%, and everything else is a ratio to that. For example: 500g flour, 350g water = 70% hydration (350÷500). This makes recipes scalable.
shortDefinition: Recipe formula where flour is 100% and everything else is a ratio.
henrysTips: Once you learn baker's percentages, you can scale any recipe up or down in your head. It's liberating!

definition: A thick plate of solid steel used as a baking surface. Because steel conducts heat 18x faster than ceramic stone, it delivers a massive blast of heat to the dough, resulting in incredible oven spring and blistering crusts.
henrysTips: If you love pizza or crusty bread, this is the best upgrade for your oven. It creates a crust that a stone simply can't match.

definition: A flat slab of ceramic or cordierite designed to hold heat and bake bread/pizza evenly. It is gentler than steel, making it better for longer bakes where you don't want the bottom to burn before the inside is cooked.

A basket used for proofing shaped bread dough, traditionally made from cane or rattan. The basket provides structure and support during the final rise and creates distinctive circular ridges on the loaf's surface.
shortDefinition: A proofing basket that gives bread its shape and texture.
henrysTips: Dust it heavily with rice flour, not regular flour. Rice flour doesn't absorb moisture, so your dough won't stick.
commonMistakes: Not flouring the basket enough, causing the dough to stick.
youtubeQuery: how to use banneton proofing basket

definition: A linen or cotton cloth cover for a proofing basket. It prevents sticky dough from getting stuck in the basket's crevices and creates a smooth surface on the loaf, which is ideal for intricate scoring.

When dough grabs onto the banneton or its liner and tears or deflates as you turn it out. It's most common with wet doughs, long cold proofs, new baskets that haven't built up a flour coating yet, and dough that's overproofed. The fix is usually better dusting, with rice flour or a rice and wheat flour mix.
shortDefinition: Dough sticking to the proofing basket when you turn it out.

troubleshooting.problem: Dough sticks even though the basket was floured
troubleshooting.solution: Switch to rice flour or a rice and wheat flour blend. Rice flour doesn't absorb water the way wheat flour does, so it stays dry between the dough and the basket.

troubleshooting.problem: New banneton sticks every time
troubleshooting.solution: Season it: dust it well, tap out the excess, and let it dry fully between bakes. It gets better with use.

troubleshooting.problem: Dough is stuck and starting to tear
troubleshooting.solution: Turn it out slowly, ease the stuck spots free with floured fingers or a bowl scraper, and bake right away.

henrysTips: Dust the top of the dough with rice flour before it goes into the basket, not just the basket. That's the side touching it.

definition: An ancient cereal grain used for food, animal feed, and malting. It contains gluten-related proteins (hordeins), so it isn't safe for celiac disease, but those proteins don't form a bread dough, so barley flour is usually blended with wheat. Malted barley is the source of diastatic and non-diastatic malt, which bakers add for enzyme activity, color, and flavor.
shortDefinition: Ancient cereal used for flour and for malt.
henrysTips: A little barley flour, around 10 to 20 percent, gives bread a mild, sweet, earthy flavor without wrecking the structure.

definition: A technique of holding back some water from the initial mix and adding it slowly later in the mixing process. This helps develop gluten faster before the dough becomes super wet.
An oval or football-shaped loaf. This shape is often preferred by bakers because it yields more uniform slices than a round boule.
henrysTips: If you want sandwiches, shape a batard. It gives you those nice, wide slices perfect for a grilled cheese.

definition: The rounded part of the loaf that expands and opens up during the bake, usually right next to the 'ear.' A big belly indicates strong fermentation and good shaping tension.
A resting period (usually 15-30 minutes) after pre-shaping. This allows the gluten to relax so the dough can be shaped into its final form without tearing or fighting back.
A flat, rectangular metal or plastic tool used to divide dough, scrape sticky bits off the counter, and help lift dough during shaping. For most bakers, it's the most-used tool on the bench.
henrysTips: If I could only have one tool, it's this. It acts like an extension of your hand when the dough is sticky.

definition: A cousin to the bagel, this round roll has a depressed center filled with cooked onions and poppy seeds. Unlike bagels, bialys are baked without being boiled first.

A stiff Italian pre-ferment made from flour, water, and a tiny amount of yeast. It is mixed into a firm dough and allowed to ferment for 12-16 hours before being added to the final dough to add complexity and strength.
henrysTips: Think of biga as a 'strength booster.' Because it's stiff, it helps add structure to wet doughs like ciabatta.
youtubeQuery: how to make biga for bread

definition: Tiny, crispy bubbles on the surface of the crust. They are highly prized by sourdough bakers and are usually achieved by a long cold fermentation (fridge proof) and a very hot bake.

When a loaf bursts open in the oven somewhere you didn't plan, usually along the side, the bottom, or the seam, instead of along your score. The gas has to go somewhere, so it escapes at the weakest spot. It often points to underproofed dough, a score that was too shallow or too timid, or a seam that wasn't sealed.
shortDefinition: A loaf bursting open in an unplanned spot in the oven.

troubleshooting.problem: Loaf tears open along the side or bottom
troubleshooting.solution: Often underproofed. Give the final proof more time and use the poke test: the dent should spring back slowly, not snap right back.

troubleshooting.problem: Score barely opened and the loaf split somewhere else
troubleshooting.solution: Score deeper and with confidence, in one smooth stroke. A tentative score seals over before the loaf finishes expanding.

troubleshooting.problem: Loaf split along the seam
troubleshooting.solution: Pinch the seam closed when shaping and proof seam side up in the banneton so it bakes seam side down.

definition: Whole-grain flour that's been sifted to remove part of the bran, landing somewhere between whole wheat and white flour. It keeps much of the flavor of the whole grain while giving a lighter, more open crumb. Many home millers bolt their flour for baguettes, country loaves, and pizza.
shortDefinition: Whole-grain flour sifted to remove some of the bran.
henrysTips: Bolted flour is my bridge for bakers who love the taste of fresh-milled but aren't ready for a dense loaf. Start there and work toward more whole grain.

definition: Sifting flour through a screen or cloth to remove some of the bran and germ. Mills have done it for centuries, and home millers do it with a sieve to get a lighter flour that still has whole-grain flavor. How much you remove depends on the screen and how many times you sift.
shortDefinition: Sifting flour to remove some of the bran.
henrysTips: Sift over a big bowl and shake gently. Weigh what's left in the sieve so you know roughly how much bran you pulled and can repeat it next time.

definition: A traditional French bread shape resembling a round ball. It is the most common shape for sourdough baked in a Dutch oven.
youtubeQuery: how to shape a sourdough boule

definition: A flexible plastic scraper with a curved edge that fits the inside of a bowl. It pulls every bit of dough out of the bowl, folds dough during bulk fermentation, and cleans dried dough off the counter. It's cheap and simple, and most bread bakers reach for it constantly.
shortDefinition: A flexible curved scraper for getting dough out of bowls.
henrysTips: Wet the scraper before you use it on sticky dough. It slides right under instead of grabbing.
youtubeQuery: how to use a bowl scraper bread

definition: Shaping dough by rolling it into strands and weaving them together. Three-strand braids are the place to start, and bakers go on to four, six, or more strands and to round braided loaves. It's best known from challah and other enriched breads, where a soft, slightly stiff dough holds the braid's pattern through proofing and baking.
shortDefinition: Weaving strands of dough into a braided loaf.
henrysTips: Roll the strands, then let them rest a few minutes before rolling them longer. Fighting a tight dough gives you strands that shrink back.
Braid loosely. The strands need room to grow, and a tight braid tends to tear at the seams.

definition: The tough outer layers of the grain kernel, rich in fiber and minerals. In bread, bran adds flavor and color but gets in the way of gluten, which is why whole-grain doughs often rise less and need more water. Sifting out some bran, grinding it finer, or soaking it ahead of time are common ways to lighten a whole-grain loaf.
shortDefinition: The fibrous outer layers of the grain kernel.
henrysTips: Don't throw away the bran you sift out. Soak it and work it back into the dough, or roll your shaped loaf in it for a rustic crust.

definition: The common explanation for why whole-grain loaves rise less: sharp bran particles are said to cut through gluten strands. Research also points to bran getting in the way of gluten in other ways, by physically interrupting the network and through compounds in the bran that interfere with gluten and compete for water. Whatever the mix of causes, finer grinding, soaking the bran, and giving the dough a longer hydration all tend to help.
shortDefinition: The idea that bran particles cut gluten and limit rise.
henrysTips: A long autolyse or fermentolyse does a lot for whole-grain dough. Give the bran time to soften before you ask the gluten to do any work.
alternateQuestions: why whole wheat bread is dense

definition: Bran mixed with water, sometimes hot, and left to hydrate before it goes into the dough. Soaking softens the bran and lets it absorb water ahead of time, so it competes less with gluten and the crumb is lighter. It's a common way to add back bran you sifted out of fresh-milled flour.
shortDefinition: Bran pre-hydrated in water before adding to dough.
henrysTips: When I sift bran out, I soak it while the main dough rests and fold it in during the first set of folds. Count the soak water in your total hydration.

definition: A high-protein flour (usually 12-14% protein) specifically milled for yeast and sourdough breads. The higher protein content helps create a strong gluten network, resulting in better rise and a chewier texture compared to all-purpose flour.
shortDefinition: High-protein flour that creates strong gluten for chewy, high-rising loaves.
henrysTips: If a recipe calls for bread flour and you only have all-purpose, expect a slightly flatter, softer loaf. Bread flour's worth keeping on hand for that chewy artisan texture.
youtubeQuery: bread flour vs all purpose flour

definition: A long knife with a serrated edge for slicing bread. The teeth saw through a hard crust without crushing the soft crumb inside, which a straight-edged knife tends to do. A long blade that's wider than your loaf makes clean, even slices much easier.
shortDefinition: A long serrated knife for slicing crusty bread.
henrysTips: Let the knife do the work with long, light strokes. Pressing down squashes the loaf.
Wait until the bread is cool before you slice. A good knife can't fix a crumb that's still setting.
youtubeQuery: how to slice crusty bread knife

definition: Bread wheat (Triticum aestivum) is the common wheat behind most of the flour on store shelves, and it makes up the vast majority of wheat grown worldwide. It's a hexaploid wheat, meaning it carries six sets of chromosomes, and it arose thousands of years ago when a cultivated tetraploid wheat crossed with a wild goatgrass. That extra set of genes is a big part of why its gluten is so elastic and good at trapping gas, which is what lets you build a tall, open loaf. Hard, soft, red, white, winter, and spring wheats are all classes of this one species.
shortDefinition: Triticum aestivum, the common wheat used for most flour.
henrysTips: When a recipe just says 'flour,' it means flour from bread wheat. Spelt, einkorn, and durum are wheat too, but they're different species and they behave differently in the bowl, so don't swap them one for one without adjusting.

definition: A highly enriched French bread with a high egg and butter content. The result is a rich, tender, and fluffy crumb with a dark, golden crust.

A German scald where grains, seeds, or flour are soaked in boiling water and left to cool before going into the dough. The hot water partly gelatinizes the starches, so they hold more water, which keeps the bread moist and helps it stay fresh longer. It's common in German whole grain and rye breads, and it should be cooled before use so it doesn't overheat the dough.
shortDefinition: A German hot-water scald of grains, seeds, or flour.
henrysTips: Make it the night before. By morning it's cool and the grains have soaked up all the water.

definition: Despite the name, buckwheat isn't wheat or even a grass. It's the seed of a plant related to rhubarb and sorrel, which makes it a pseudocereal. It's gluten-free (unless cross-contaminated) and has a strong, earthy flavor. It's traditional in Breton galettes, Russian blini, Japanese soba, and kasha, and in bread it's usually blended with wheat because it can't build a gluten network.
shortDefinition: Gluten-free seed, not wheat, used like a grain.
henrysTips: Buckwheat's flavor is bold. About 10 to 20 percent in a sourdough loaf is plenty for most people.

definition: The first rise of bread dough after mixing, where the entire mass of dough ferments together in one container before being divided and shaped. This is when most of the flavor and structure development happens.
shortDefinition: The first rise before shaping, where flavor develops.
henrysTips: Watch the dough, not the clock. A 4-hour bulk fermentation at 78°F is not the same as 4 hours at 68°F.

troubleshooting.problem: Dough isn't rising during bulk
troubleshooting.solution: Check your starter strength, room temperature, and dough temperature. Cold dough ferments slowly.

definition: The amount of volume increase you aim for during bulk fermentation before shaping. Depending on flour, temperature, and how much starter or yeast you use, targets often fall somewhere around 30% to 100%. A number is a helpful guide, but reading the dough matters more: a domed surface, a jiggly wobble, bubbles along the sides of the container, and a lighter, airier feel.
shortDefinition: How much the dough should rise during bulk fermentation.
henrysTips: Fresh-milled and whole grain doughs often can't rise as high as white flour doughs before they start to weaken, so don't chase a big number with them. Trust the jiggle and the bubbles.
alternateQuestions: how much should dough rise in bulk
youtubeQuery: how to know when bulk fermentation is done sourdough

definition: The browning of sugars by heat alone, creating sweet, nutty, slightly bitter flavors and a deeper color. It's different from the Maillard reaction, which needs amino acids from proteins along with sugars and starts at lower temperatures. In a bread crust both happen together, which is why a well-baked, deeply browned crust tastes so much richer than a pale one.
shortDefinition: Browning of sugars by heat, separate from Maillard browning.
henrysTips: Don't pull your bread too early. That dark, bold crust is where caramelization and Maillard flavor live.
youtubeQuery: caramelization vs maillard reaction bread crust

definition: A heavy iron pan that holds and spreads heat well. Bakers use it on the stovetop for flatbreads like naan and pita and for English muffins, and in the oven for pan pizza, focaccia, and skillet breads. Its thick mass keeps the heat steady when cold dough hits it, which helps with browning and a crisp bottom.
shortDefinition: A heavy iron pan that holds heat for flatbreads and pan breads.
henrysTips: Preheat it longer than you think, especially for flatbreads. A skillet that's only hot in the middle cooks unevenly.

definition: A braided, enriched bread of Jewish origin, traditionally eaten on Shabbat. It is made with eggs and oil (but no butter/dairy if kosher) and has a soft, sweet crumb.
An Italian white bread made from a very wet (high hydration) dough. It is known for its flat, slipper-like shape and extremely open, airy crumb.
henrysTips: Don't try to shape this like a normal loaf! It's mostly just gently folding a wet puddle of dough into a rectangle.

definition: Clear flour is what's left of the white flour after the patent flour has been taken out. It comes from parts of the endosperm closer to the bran, so it's a bit darker, higher in ash, and often higher in protein than patent flour. Bakers have long used it in rye breads, especially deli-style rye, where its strength helps support weak rye dough and its color doesn't matter.
shortDefinition: Darker, higher-ash flour left after patent is removed.
henrysTips: If an old deli rye recipe calls for clear flour and you can't find it, bread flour is a workable stand-in. The loaf will just be a little lighter in color and flavor.

definition: A bell-shaped ceramic or cast iron cover used to bake bread. Like a Dutch oven, it traps steam around the loaf to create a superior crust and oven spring.
A gentle folding technique where you lift the center of the dough and let the sides fall underneath, then rotate 90° and repeat. It builds strength without degassing the dough.
shortDefinition: A gentle folding technique that builds dough strength.
henrysTips: This is my go-to for high-hydration doughs. It's gentler than stretch-and-fold and perfect for preserving those bubbles.

definition: Doing part or all of bulk fermentation in the refrigerator instead of at room temperature. The cold slows fermentation way down, which gives you more control over timing and usually deepens flavor. Many bakers let the dough rise partway at room temperature first, then finish bulk in the fridge before dividing and shaping.
shortDefinition: Running bulk fermentation partly in the fridge.
henrysTips: Cold bulk is great for busy schedules. Just remember cold dough is stiffer, so shaping takes a gentler, firmer hand, and the dough may need time to warm up a bit.

definition: Proofing shaped dough in the refrigerator overnight (or up to 72 hours). The cold slows fermentation dramatically, allowing for extended flavor development while fitting your schedule.
shortDefinition: Slow final rise in the refrigerator overnight.
henrysTips: This is my default method. Shape before bed, bake first thing in the morning. Plus, cold dough scores beautifully.

definition: An Italian Easter bread baked in the shape of a dove, the symbol of peace. It's made with methods much like panettone: a rich, slow-fermented dough, traditionally leavened with lievito madre and built over more than one dough stage. It usually holds candied orange peel and is topped with an almond glaze, whole almonds, and pearl sugar.
shortDefinition: Italian dove-shaped Easter bread topped with almond glaze.
henrysTips: If you've made panettone, you're most of the way there. Get your starter strong and active days ahead, because these doughs ask a lot of it.

definition: A cast iron set consisting of a deep pot and a shallow skillet lid that lock together. Bakers flip it upside down, using the shallow skillet as the base, which makes loading the dough much safer and easier than a deep Dutch oven.
henrysTips: I like this better than a regular Dutch oven because you don't have to drop the dough down a deep pot and risk burning your knuckles.

definition: A wire grid that allows air to circulate under the hot bread. Cooling bread on a rack prevents the bottom from getting soggy due to condensation.

Dried corn ground into a coarse, medium, or fine meal. Corn has no gluten-forming proteins, so cornmeal can't build a dough on its own. Bakers use it for cornbread, for dusting peels and pans so loaves slide and don't stick, and in breads like New England anadama, made with cornmeal and molasses. Masa harina is different: the corn is nixtamalized, cooked and soaked in an alkaline solution, which changes it so it forms a pliable dough for tortillas.
shortDefinition: Ground dried corn; gluten-free, used for cornbread and dusting.
henrysTips: For dusting a peel, I like a mix of cornmeal and semolina or rice flour. It rolls like ball bearings and the dough slides right off.
alternateQuestions: Is cornmeal the same as masa harina?

definition: Whole grain broken into coarse pieces rather than ground into flour. It adds chew and a rustic look to bread. Because the pieces are hard and take up water slowly, they're usually soaked or cooked before going into the dough so they don't stay crunchy or pull water from it.
shortDefinition: Whole grain broken into coarse pieces, not flour.
henrysTips: Soak cracked grain overnight, or pour hot water over it, then drain well before adding it. Dry cracked grain in a dough is like little rocks.

definition: A crescent or straight roll made from yeasted, laminated dough: a butter block folded into the dough over several turns to build many thin layers. In the oven the butter's water turns to steam and puffs those layers apart into a shattering crust and a honeycomb inside. It's closely tied to France, with roots often traced to the Viennese kipferl, and it's one of the harder things a home baker can learn.
shortDefinition: A flaky crescent roll made from yeasted laminated dough.
henrysTips: Keep everything cold, and don't rush the proof. Underproofed croissants leak butter in the oven and come out dense.
Your first batch won't be perfect. Bake them anyway, because they'll still be better than most you can buy.

definition: A simple 'X' cut across the top of a round boule. It is one of the most effective scores for beginners because it allows the bread to open evenly in four directions, preventing 'blowouts' on the side.
henrysTips: When in doubt, X marks the spot. It's reliable and maximizes that oven spring.

definition: The internal texture and structure of bread, referring to the pattern of holes, their size, and how the bread feels when you bite into it. 'Open crumb' has large, irregular holes, while 'tight crumb' is more uniform and dense.
shortDefinition: The interior texture and hole structure of bread.
henrysTips: Don't obsess over giant holes. Good crumb is about eating quality, not Instagram photos.

definition: The hard, caramelized outer shell of the bread. A good artisan crust should be dark, blistered, and crisp, singing with flavor from the Maillard reaction.

Starch granules that get cracked or broken during milling. Damaged starch absorbs much more water than intact starch and is easier for amylase enzymes to break into sugars. A moderate amount helps water absorption and fermentation, but too much can make a dough slack and sticky and the crumb gummy.
shortDefinition: Starch granules broken during milling that soak up more water.
henrysTips: If a very finely milled dough turns sticky late in bulk, damaged starch and enzymes are often part of the story. Cut the ferment a little shorter next time.

definition: A mixing tool with a long handle and a stiff, looped wire head. It is designed to cut through thick, heavy doughs without getting clogged like a standard balloon whisk.
henrysTips: A regular whisk will get gummed up instantly. This thing powers through flour and water like magic.

definition: Pressing or knocking some of the gas out of fermented dough. Sometimes it's on purpose: a gentle degas before shaping evens out the bubbles, and sandwich loaves are often degassed more firmly for a tighter, even crumb. Sometimes it's an accident, when rough handling flattens the bubbles you worked hours to build and the crumb ends up tighter than you wanted.
shortDefinition: Pressing gas out of fermented dough, on purpose or not.
henrysTips: For an open crumb, handle the dough like it's full of something you don't want to spill. For a soft sandwich loaf, press it out more firmly and you'll get that even slice.

definition: A bread interior that lacks air bubbles and feels heavy or brick-like. It is one of the most common issues for beginners.
henrysTips: If your starter wasn't doubling in size before you used it, your bread will likely be dense. Healthy starter = airy bread.

troubleshooting.problem: Heavy, tight crumb with few holes
troubleshooting.solution: Most often underfermentation. Make sure your starter is peaking and let bulk go until the dough is airy and domed, not just by the clock.

troubleshooting.problem: Dense and flat, spreads on the counter
troubleshooting.solution: Overproofing or weak gluten. Add a set of folds, shorten the final proof, or cold proof so you have more control.

troubleshooting.problem: Dense whole grain loaf
troubleshooting.solution: Whole grain flour needs more water and often a shorter fermentation. Try an autolyse or a bran soaker and watch the dough closely.

definition: A formula used by bakers to calculate exactly how hot or cold their water needs to be to hit a specific dough temperature (usually 75-78°F) after mixing. Controlling this keeps fermentation timing consistent regardless of the season.
henrysTips: If you bake bread in summer and winter and get wildly different results, it's because you aren't managing your DDT. The dough cares about its own temperature, not the room temperature.

definition: A thick, rectangular pizza baked in a well-oiled steel pan. Cheese goes all the way to the edges so it melts down the pan's sides and fries into a crisp, lacy, caramelized frico crust. The sauce often goes on top, sometimes in stripes, and the traditional cheese is Wisconsin brick cheese. The dough is wet and airy, closer to focaccia than to thin-crust pizza.
shortDefinition: Rectangular pan pizza with a crisp cheese edge.
henrysTips: Push the cheese right against the walls of the pan. That crispy cheese edge is the whole point.
youtubeQuery: Detroit style pizza pan frico crust

definition: A powder made from sprouted barley that is rich in enzymes (amylase). Adding a small amount to dough helps break down starch into sugar, promoting a faster rise and better browning.
henrysTips: Check your flour bag first. Most US all-purpose and bread flours already have malted barley flour added. It's the unmalted flours, like many organic and imported ones, where a pinch can boost rise and crust color.

definition: A kitchen scale used to weigh ingredients by gram rather than volume. Weighing matters in bread baking because a cup of flour can vary wildly in weight depending on how it's scooped.
henrysTips: Ditch the cups! A scale is the single biggest upgrade you can make to your baking consistency.
commonMistakes: Using measuring cups for flour and wondering why the dough is too dry.

definition: Pricking a flat dough (like crackers, pizza, or focaccia) with a fork or roller to create small holes. These holes prevent large air bubbles from ballooning up during the bake.

A clear container with straight sides, and often volume markings, used for bulk fermentation. Because the sides are straight, you can see exactly how much the dough has grown and judge your bulk rise by percentage. Clear sides also let you see bubbles forming along the edges and bottom, which tells you a lot about fermentation.
shortDefinition: A clear, straight-sided tub for tracking bulk rise.
henrysTips: Put a strip of tape on the side at the dough's starting level. Then you're reading the rise, not guessing it.

definition: A machine that rolls dough out to an even, set thickness by passing it between rollers, a little thinner with each pass. Bakeries use them for laminated doughs like croissant and puff pastry, and for pizza bases, crackers, and flatbreads. They save a lot of rolling-pin work and give the same thickness every time, which matters a lot in laminated dough.
shortDefinition: A machine that rolls dough to an even thickness.
henrysTips: You don't need one to make great croissants at home. A good rolling pin, cold dough, and patience will get you there.

definition: Durum (Triticum turgidum subsp. durum) is a very hard, amber-colored wheat best known for pasta. Semolina is its coarse meal, and durum rimacinata is semolina that's been re-milled fine for bread, the base of many Sicilian-style loaves. Durum's gluten is strong but not very extensible, and its golden crumb comes from natural carotenoid pigments.
shortDefinition: Hard amber wheat behind semolina and pasta.
henrysTips: For bread, look for fine durum (rimacinata), not coarse semolina. The coarse stuff is better for dusting peels than for building a loaf.

definition: A heavy cast-iron pot with a tight-fitting lid, used to create a steamy baking environment that mimics a professional steam-injected oven. The trapped steam keeps the crust soft initially, allowing maximum oven spring.
shortDefinition: Cast iron pot that traps steam for better bread.
henrysTips: Preheat it empty at 500°F for at least 30 minutes. A cold Dutch oven won't give you that explosive spring.

definition: The dramatic flap of crust that rises up along a properly executed score line. It's created by scoring at a shallow angle (about 30°) with a sharp blade, allowing the bread to open sideways instead of straight up.
shortDefinition: The raised flap of crust along the score line.
henrysTips: Angle is everything. Hold your lame at 30° to the surface, not straight down. That's the secret to a good ear.
youtubeQuery: how to get an ear on sourdough

definition: Beaten egg, often thinned with a little water, milk, or cream, brushed on dough before baking. It gives the crust shine and deeper browning, and it works as glue for seeds and toppings. Whole egg gives a golden shine, yolk gives deeper color, and white alone gives shine with less browning.
shortDefinition: Beaten egg brushed on dough for shine and color.
henrysTips: Add a pinch of salt and strain it. It brushes on thinner and smoother, with no streaks.
Don't let it pool in the creases. Puddles of egg bake into dark spots and can glue the dough down so it can't rise.
youtubeQuery: egg wash for bread shiny crust

definition: Einkorn (Triticum monococcum) is one of the earliest domesticated wheats, with small kernels and a single grain per spikelet. It has a sweet, nutty flavor and a golden color from its natural carotenoids. It does contain gluten, but that gluten is weak and sticky, so einkorn doughs don't build the strength or rise of bread wheat. It usually wants less water than you'd guess, short and gentle mixing, and a pan or a modest free-form loaf.
shortDefinition: Early domesticated wheat with weak, sticky gluten.
henrysTips: Treat einkorn gently. Mix just until it comes together, skip the long kneading and slap-and-folds, and start with less water than your usual recipe. It'll feel wetter as it rests.
My einkorn loaves come out best in a loaf pan. The pan does the structural work the gluten can't.

definition: The ability of dough to spring back to its original shape after being stretched. While you want some stretch (extensibility), you need elasticity so the loaf holds its shape and doesn't pancake in the oven.
shortDefinition: The dough's ability to snap back and hold its shape.
henrysTips: Think of elasticity like a rubber band. You need enough tension to hold the gas bubbles in, but not so much that it fights you.

definition: Emmer (Triticum dicoccum, also written T. turgidum subsp. dicoccum) is an ancient hulled wheat and a relative of durum. It has a rich, earthy flavor and medium-strength gluten that tends to be less elastic than modern bread wheat. In the US, most grain sold as farro is emmer. Bakers often blend it with bread flour, or use it in whole grain loaves and flatbreads.
shortDefinition: Ancient hulled wheat, the usual farro in the US.
henrysTips: Emmer dough can feel strong early and then slacken during bulk, so I watch the dough more than the clock.

definition: The largest part of the grain kernel, made mostly of starch with the proteins that form gluten. White flour comes from the endosperm alone, which is why it's milder, lighter, and keeps longer than whole-grain flour. The center of the endosperm usually gives the whitest, finest flour, while the outer parts carry more protein and minerals.
shortDefinition: The starchy inner part of the kernel that makes white flour.
henrysTips: When I explain flour to new bakers, I say white flour is just the endosperm. Whole wheat puts the bran and germ back.

definition: A small, round, flat yeast bread that is cooked on a griddle or skillet rather than in an oven. They are famous for their 'nooks and crannies' interior, perfect for holding butter.
henrysTips: Always split these with a fork, never a knife! Cutting them ruins the nooks and crannies.

definition: Dough that contains significant amounts of fat, sugar, dairy, or eggs (like Brioche or Challah). These ingredients inhibit gluten development and yeast activity, so these doughs often take longer to rise.
henrysTips: Sugar and fat slow down yeast (the 'osmotic stress'). Be patient; enriched doughs operate on their own slow timeline.

definition: The ability of dough to stretch without tearing. An extensible dough relaxes and lengthens easily (like bubblegum), which is what you need for shaping baguettes or stretching pizza.
shortDefinition: How much the dough can stretch before it snaps or tears.
henrysTips: If your dough keeps shrinking back when you try to roll it out, it lacks extensibility. Let it rest for 10 minutes to relax the gluten, then try again.
alternateQuestions: Why does my dough shrink back?

definition: The share of the whole grain that ends up in the flour, as a percentage of the grain's weight. Whole-grain flour is close to 100 percent, while white flour keeps only part of the kernel, often roughly 70 to 75 percent. Higher extraction means more bran, germ, minerals, and flavor, plus more water absorption and a heavier dough.
shortDefinition: Percentage of the whole grain kept in the flour.
henrysTips: At home you can estimate it yourself: weigh the flour before sifting and the bran you pull out. What passes through the sieve is your extraction.
alternateQuestions: what does extraction mean in flour

definition: Falling number is a lab test for alpha-amylase activity, the enzyme that breaks starch into sugars. A flour and water slurry is heated, and the test measures how many seconds a stirrer takes to fall through it. A low number means lots of enzyme activity, often from sprout damage, and that flour can give a sticky, gummy crumb. A high number means little activity, which can mean slow fermentation and a pale crust, and mills often correct it by adding malted barley flour. Mills usually aim for a middle range for bread flour.
shortDefinition: Seconds-based test of a flour's starch-eating enzymes.
henrysTips: Home millers can't run a falling number test, but your bread will hint at it. If a new batch of berries suddenly gives you a sticky crumb with no other changes, enzyme activity is a good suspect.

definition: An Italian name for hulled ancient wheat that isn't one single species. Depending on the region and the seller, farro can mean einkorn (farro piccolo), emmer (farro medio), or spelt (farro grande). Emmer is the most common meaning in the US. Whole farro is usually cooked as a grain or added to bread as a soaker, and milled farro behaves like the wheat it actually is, so check the label for the species.
shortDefinition: Italian name for einkorn, emmer, or spelt grain.
henrysTips: Cooked farro folded into a sourdough loaf is one of my favorite inclusions. Cool it and drain it well first so it doesn't make the dough slack.
alternateQuestions: Is farro the same as spelt?

definition: The process of adding fresh flour and water to your sourdough starter to keep the yeast and bacteria alive and active. Also called 'refreshing' the starter.
shortDefinition: Adding fresh flour and water to keep starter alive.
henrysTips: I do 1:1:1 (starter:water:flour) for maintenance. Simple and consistent.

definition: The proportion of starter to fresh flour and water when you feed it, written starter:flour:water by weight. A 1:1:1 feeding is equal parts of each, while something like 1:5:5 uses a small amount of starter with much more food. Bigger ratios usually take longer to reach peak and tend to give milder flavor, so you can pick a ratio to fit your schedule and your kitchen's temperature.
shortDefinition: How much starter, flour, and water you combine at a feeding.
henrysTips: I maintain my starter at 1:1:1 because it fits my day. When I need it to wait longer, say overnight or while I'm out, I'll stretch the ratio so it peaks when I'm ready for it.
alternateQuestions: how much to feed sourdough starter

definition: The biological process where yeast and bacteria consume sugars in the dough and produce carbon dioxide (which makes the bread rise), alcohol, and organic acids (which create flavor).
shortDefinition: The process where yeast creates gas and flavor.
henrysTips: Temperature is everything. 76-78°F is the sweet spot for most doughs.

definition: Henry's technique from 'Sourdough for the Rest of Us' - an autolyse that includes the sourdough starter. Mix flour, water, and starter, then let it rest before adding salt. This gives you the benefits of autolyse while fermentation begins.
shortDefinition: Autolyse with starter included (Henry's method).
henrysTips: This is how I teach it in my book. It simplifies the process and you still get incredible gluten development.
bookRef: Sourdough for the Rest of Us

definition: A simple test to check if your sourdough starter is active and ready to use. Drop a spoonful of starter in water. If it floats, it's full of gas and ready to bake with. If it sinks, it needs more time or another feeding.
shortDefinition: Test to see if starter is ready by floating it in water.
henrysTips: Use room temperature water for the test. Cold water can give false negatives.
Don't treat it as gospel. Whole grain, rye, and very wet starters can be ready to bake and still sink. Trust the rise, the bubbles, and the smell too.

definition: How recently flour was milled and how well it's kept. Whole-grain and fresh-milled flours contain germ oils that can go rancid, giving a bitter, stale, or paint-like smell. Store them cool and airtight, and move them to the fridge or freezer if you won't use them soon. White flour keeps longer because the germ and bran have been removed.
shortDefinition: How recently flour was milled and how well it's stored.
henrysTips: I keep whole-grain flour in the freezer in sealed bags. Let it come up toward room temperature before mixing so it doesn't chill your dough.
Smell your flour before you bake. Fresh whole wheat smells sweet and nutty. Sharp or bitter means it's time to toss it.
alternateQuestions: how to store whole wheat flour

definition: Flour strength is a flour's ability to form a dough that resists stretching, holds its shape, and keeps trapping gas over time. It comes from both protein content and gluten quality. Strong flours handle higher hydration, longer fermentation, and heavy enrichment like butter and sugar, while weak flours are better for quick doughs, flatbreads, and pastry. Bakers in Europe often describe strength with the alveograph's W value.
shortDefinition: A flour's power to build and hold a gassy dough.
henrysTips: Match flour strength to the job. A long cold ferment or a buttery brioche needs a strong flour to stay standing, but that same flour can make a quick flatbread tough and springy.
alternateQuestions: what does strong bread flour mean

definition: A defect where the top crust separates from the crumb, creating a large gap or 'cave' at the top of the loaf. It makes the bread difficult to slice for sandwiches.

troubleshooting.problem: Crust lifts off the bread
troubleshooting.solution: Often the dough dried out during proofing and formed a skin. Cover it well.

troubleshooting.problem: Big gap under the top crust
troubleshooting.solution: Can also come from underproofing, trapping air or excess flour while shaping, or a bake that sets the top crust before the inside catches up. Shape tightly, brush off extra flour, and proof fully.

definition: An oven-baked Italian flatbread similar in style to pizza dough. It is usually dimpled with fingers and drizzled with olive oil and herbs before baking.
henrysTips: The easiest bread to start with! No shaping required. Just pour it in a pan, dimple it with your fingers, and bake.

definition: A tiny-grained millet that's been grown in West Africa for a very long time, in places like Senegal, Mali, and Guinea, and holds a respected place in many of the region's food traditions. It's gluten-free with a light, slightly nutty flavor, and the cleaned grain cooks very fast, in just a few minutes. Bakers use fonio flour in gluten-free blends or as a small addition to wheat breads.
shortDefinition: Fast-cooking, gluten-free West African grain.

definition: A crumb with big, irregular holes that looks open at first glance, but the bread around those holes is dense, tight, or gummy. It usually comes from underfermented dough: a few large pockets of gas form while the rest of the dough never got enough fermentation to open up. Bakers sometimes mistake it for a great open crumb.
shortDefinition: Big holes in an underfermented loaf with dense crumb between.

troubleshooting.problem: Large holes with tight, dense crumb between them
troubleshooting.solution: Let bulk fermentation go longer. Judge it by volume increase, a domed and jiggly dough, and bubbles on the sides, not by the clock.

troubleshooting.problem: Fermentation is slow every time
troubleshooting.solution: Check your dough temperature and your starter. A cool kitchen or a starter used before it peaks can stretch fermentation well past what the recipe says.

troubleshooting.problem: Big tunnel just under the top crust
troubleshooting.solution: That's often underfermentation too, sometimes with loose shaping. Ferment fully and shape with enough tension.

henrysTips: An even, open crumb has bubbles of many sizes all through it, with a shiny, almost lacy look. If the holes look like caves in a brick, give fermentation more time.
alternateQuestions: why does my bread have big holes

definition: A flat bread from Provence in southern France, cut and stretched open so it looks like a leaf or an ear of wheat. It's often brushed with olive oil and flavored with herbs, olives, or cheese. The cuts give it a lot of crust for its size, and it's a cousin of Italian focaccia.
shortDefinition: A Provençal flatbread cut and stretched into a leaf shape.
henrysTips: After you make the cuts, pull them open wide. They close up more than you'd expect as the dough proofs and bakes.

definition: Also known as 'cake yeast,' this is moist, perishable yeast sold in compressed blocks. It is highly active and preferred by professional bakeries for its sweet flavor and powerful rising ability, especially in high-sugar doughs.
henrysTips: It smells amazing, like fresh apples and beer, but it spoils in two weeks. Stick to instant yeast unless you bake every single day.

definition: Flour ground from whole grain shortly before you bake with it, so it still carries all of the bran, germ, and endosperm and their natural oils and enzymes. It tastes noticeably fuller than bagged flour, but it behaves differently: it often takes up water more slowly, can need more of it, and may ferment faster because of its higher enzyme activity. Expect to adjust hydration and timing rather than follow a white-flour recipe as written.
shortDefinition: Whole-grain flour ground at or near the time of baking.
henrysTips: When I switch a recipe to fresh-milled flour, I hold back some of the water, give the dough a rest, and then add more as it absorbs. It drinks slower than you'd think.
Watch the dough, not the clock. Fresh-milled doughs often move faster in bulk than the same recipe made with store-bought flour.
youtubeQuery: baking bread with fresh milled flour

definition: The amount of heat generated by the friction of a mixer or hand-kneading. Professional bakers subtract this number from their water temperature calculation to prevent the dough from overheating during the mix.
The process where starch granules absorb water and swell up when heated (during baking). This sets the structure of the bread crumb, turning it from liquid dough into solid bread.

The small embryo of the grain kernel, the part that would sprout into a new plant. It holds most of the grain's oil along with vitamins and enzymes, which adds flavor but is also why whole-grain flour can go rancid. White flour is milled without it, and some bakers find that germ compounds can soften a dough slightly.
shortDefinition: The oil-rich embryo of the grain kernel.
henrysTips: That nutty smell when you open a bag of fresh-milled flour is mostly the germ. If it smells like old crayons or paint instead, the oils have turned.

definition: A network of proteins (primarily gliadin and glutenin) that forms when wheat flour is mixed with water. This elastic network traps gas bubbles produced during fermentation, allowing bread to rise and giving it structure.
shortDefinition: The protein network that gives bread structure.
henrysTips: You don't need to knead sourdough like traditional bread. Folds during bulk fermentation do most of the work.

definition: Gluten quality describes how well a flour's proteins behave once they form gluten: how strong, stretchy, and stable the network is, and how well it holds gas over a long ferment. It depends on the kinds of proteins in the wheat, especially the balance between the elastic glutenins and the stretchy gliadins, not just how much protein there is. That's why einkorn can test high in protein yet make a soft, slack dough, while a modern bread wheat with similar protein stands up tall.
shortDefinition: How well gluten performs, separate from how much there is.
henrysTips: Don't judge a flour by the protein number alone. Mix a small test batch, do a windowpane, and watch how it holds up during bulk. The dough will tell you about gluten quality faster than the label will.

definition: A countertop appliance used to grind whole berries (wheat, rye, spelt) into fresh flour at home. Home mills are either impact mills, which shatter grain with fast-spinning fins, or stone and burr mills, which grind it between plates. Freshly milled flour ferments much faster and has a distinctively sweet, grassy flavor.
A texture fault where the inside of the bread feels damp, sticky, or doughy even after cooling. It often balls up when you chew it.

troubleshooting.problem: Bread is sticky inside
troubleshooting.solution: Wait for the loaf to cool completely before slicing. Cutting hot bread releases steam that should stay inside to set the crumb.

troubleshooting.problem: Gummy even after cooling
troubleshooting.solution: Likely underbaked. Bake until the center reads 205-210°F on a probe thermometer and the crust is deep brown.

troubleshooting.problem: Gummy streak or dense band near the bottom
troubleshooting.solution: Often underfermentation, or a rye or fresh-milled dough with high enzyme activity. Ferment fully, and for rye use enough sourdough acidity.

definition: Hard red spring wheat is planted in spring and harvested in late summer, mainly in the northern US plains and Canada where winters are too harsh for fall planting. It usually runs among the highest in protein of the US classes, so it's prized for strong bread flours, bagels, and for blending into weaker flours to give them more strength. Dough made from it often takes more water and more mixing to reach full development.
shortDefinition: Spring-planted hard wheat, usually very high in protein.
henrysTips: When I want a chewy bagel or a loaf that holds up to a long cold proof, spring wheat flour is where I reach. Give it a little extra water and a little extra time to come together.

definition: Hard red winter wheat is planted in the fall, sits through winter, and is harvested the next summer. It's the largest US wheat class and is grown mostly across the Great Plains. It has moderate to fairly high protein and a reddish bran, and it's the workhorse behind a lot of all-purpose and bread flour. In whole wheat form it has the familiar, hearty wheat flavor many people know from whole wheat bread.
shortDefinition: Fall-planted hard wheat behind much US bread and AP flour.
henrysTips: Hard red winter is a great all-rounder for home milling. It's strong enough for bread but not so tight that it fights you, which makes it a good berry to learn on.

definition: Hard wheat has a kernel with a firm, glassy endosperm where the starch and protein are bound tightly together. When it's milled it breaks into coarser, gritty particles and creates more damaged starch, so its flour usually soaks up more water. Hard wheats also tend to carry more protein, which is why bread flour comes from them, but hardness is about kernel texture, not protein. The two usually travel together without being the same thing.
shortDefinition: Wheat with a firm kernel, usually higher in protein.
henrysTips: If you're milling at home for sandwich loaves or hearth bread, start with a hard wheat berry. Expect fresh-milled hard wheat to drink more water than the white flour you're used to, so hold some back and add it as the dough tells you.

definition: Hard white wheat has the same firm kernel and bread-worthy protein as hard red wheat, but its bran is pale. Red wheat's bran carries pigments and phenolic compounds that give whole wheat its darker color and slightly bitter edge, and white wheat has much less of them. The result is a whole wheat flour that's lighter in color and milder in flavor, which is why it's so popular with home millers and with families who aren't sold on whole wheat yet.
shortDefinition: Hard wheat with pale bran for milder, lighter whole wheat.
henrysTips: If your kids turn their noses up at whole wheat bread, mill hard white wheat and don't say a word. It still has all the bran and germ, it just tastes gentler.
White wheat bran still absorbs water and still gets in the way of gluten, so treat it like any other whole grain flour when you set your hydration.

definition: Any bread baked directly on the hot floor of an oven (or on a pizza stone/steel) rather than in a pan. These loaves typically have a thicker, crustier bottom.

A grain variety grown before the big wave of modern wheat breeding in the mid 1900s and kept alive by farmers, seed savers, and small mills. Red Fife, Turkey Red, Sonora, and Rouge de Bordeaux are common heritage wheats in North America. Heritage and heirloom overlap and are used loosely, so neither has a legal definition. For bakers, these wheats often bring more flavor and color but weaker or less predictable gluten than modern bread flour.
shortDefinition: Older grain varieties preserved from before modern breeding.
henrysTips: Heritage flours change from harvest to harvest. When I open a new bag, I hold back some of the water and add it during mixing once I see how the dough takes it.
alternateQuestions: What's the difference between heritage and heirloom grain?

definition: Flour that keeps more of the bran and germ than white flour but less than whole wheat, usually made by sifting out only the coarsest bran. It gives a darker, more flavorful loaf that still rises well. It's a common choice for country loaves and hearth breads.
shortDefinition: Flour between whole wheat and white, with some bran removed.
henrysTips: If your whole-wheat loaves feel heavy, try a high-extraction flour. You give up a little fiber and get back a lot of lift.

definition: A long, flat Italian-American roll with a soft interior and a slightly crisp crust, designed to hold heavy sandwich fillings without falling apart.

Grinding whole grains into flour in your own kitchen with a countertop mill. It lets you choose the grain, the variety, and how fine or coarse the flour is, and you bake with flour at its freshest. The trade-offs are a learning curve, since fresh whole-grain flour handles differently, and the need to store berries and flour properly.
shortDefinition: Grinding your own flour from whole grain at home.
henrysTips: I mill at home with an impact mill, and I only grind what I need for the bake in front of me. Whole berries keep far better than flour does.
Start with one grain you know, like hard red wheat, and bake the same loaf a few times before you start swapping varieties.
alternateQuestions: how to mill your own flour
youtubeQuery: home milling flour for bread beginners

definition: The grayish or brownish liquid that forms on top of a neglected or hungry sourdough starter. It's mostly alcohol produced by the yeast. You can stir it back in or pour it off before feeding.
shortDefinition: Liquid on hungry starter (alcohol from yeast).
henrysTips: Hooch means your starter ran out of food. Feed it more often, or feed it a bigger ratio of fresh flour and water so it lasts longer between feedings.

troubleshooting.problem: Dark hooch forming daily
troubleshooting.solution: Your starter is going hungry between feedings. Feed at a bigger ratio (1:3:3 or 1:5:5 starter:flour:water), feed twice a day, or keep it somewhere cooler.

definition: The ratio of water to flour in dough, expressed as a percentage using baker's math. A dough with 500g flour and 375g water has 75% hydration (375÷500=0.75). Higher hydration typically means more open crumb but stickier dough.
shortDefinition: The percentage of water to flour in dough.
henrysTips: Start at 70% hydration and work your way up. Don't jump straight to 85% and wonder why you're wrestling with soup.

definition: Grain that's kept separate and traceable from the field to the mill, so you know the variety and often the farm and harvest it came from. Most commodity wheat is blended from many farms and sold by class and grade. Identity-preserved grain lets small mills and bakers choose specific varieties and growers, which matters when you care about flavor, terroir, or consistent performance from one lot.
shortDefinition: Grain kept separate and traceable from farm to mill.

definition: A grain mill that uses steel fins or rows of teeth spinning at high speed to shatter kernels, rather than grinding them between two surfaces. It's fast and turns out fine flour with little effort, which is why it's popular for home bread baking. Most impact mills generally can't handle oily seeds and nuts or very wet or damp material, and many give you less control over very coarse grinds than a stone or burr mill.
shortDefinition: A fast mill that shatters grain with high-speed steel fins.
henrysTips: My everyday mill is an impact mill. It's loud, but it's quick and the flour comes out fine enough for most of my breads.
Keep flax, nuts, and anything oily or damp out of an impact mill unless the maker says it's fine. Check your manual.
youtubeQuery: impact grain mill vs stone mill

definition: Any solid ingredients added to the dough, such as nuts, seeds, dried fruit, cheese, or olives. These are usually added during the lamination or folding stage.
henrysTips: Don't add these too early during mixing, or they might shred your gluten network. Fold them in gently after the dough has developed some strength.

definition: A 'point-and-shoot' laser thermometer that reads surface temperatures instantly. It's the quickest way to check if your baking stone or steel is hot enough (500°F+) before launching your bread.

A spongy, slightly sour flatbread at the center of Ethiopian and Eritrean meals, traditionally made from teff. The batter ferments for a few days, then it's poured onto a large round griddle and cooked on one side only, covered, so the top sets full of tiny holes called eyes. Injera is both plate and utensil: stews are served on top of it, and you tear off pieces to scoop up food, usually sharing from one platter.
shortDefinition: Spongy fermented teff flatbread of Ethiopia and Eritrea.
henrysTips: Learn it from people who grew up with it if you can. Getting the eyes right takes a feel for the batter that recipes struggle to put into words.

definition: The percentage of sourdough starter added to a dough recipe. A 'high inoculation' (20%+) makes the dough rise faster, while a 'low inoculation' (<10%) allows for a very long, slow fermentation.

A fast-acting dry yeast that can be mixed directly into flour without dissolving in water first. It is more potent than active dry yeast and is the preferred choice for most modern bread recipes because of its reliability and speed.
henrysTips: I use this exclusively. You don't need to 'bloom' it in warm water. Just toss it in the bowl and go. It's foolproof.
alternateQuestions: Rapid rise yeast vs instant yeast

definition: A mixing method involving high speed and long duration to fully develop gluten mechanically. It's the go-to method for enriched doughs (like Brioche) where fat inhibits gluten formation, requiring the mixer to do the hard work.
A round, crusty Austrian roll characterized by a 5-point pinwheel pattern on top. It is traditionally made by folding the dough corners into the center, though stamps are often used today.

Khorasan (Triticum turgidum subsp. turanicum) is an ancient wheat with large golden kernels and a buttery, sweet flavor. KAMUT® is a trademarked brand of khorasan wheat grown under specific standards, so all KAMUT® is khorasan but not all khorasan can be sold as KAMUT®. Its protein is often high, but the gluten tends to be weaker and less elastic than modern bread wheat, so the dough can feel extensible and slack.
shortDefinition: Large-kerneled ancient wheat, sold as the KAMUT® brand.
henrysTips: Don't read the protein number on khorasan and expect bread flour strength. Use extra folds, and blend it with bread flour if you want a taller loaf.

definition: The traditional method of working dough by repeatedly folding, pressing, and stretching it to develop gluten structure. Can be done by hand or with a mixer.
shortDefinition: Working dough to develop gluten structure.
henrysTips: With sourdough, you rarely need to knead. The long fermentation time develops gluten naturally with just a few folds.

definition: A German cooked paste of flour or grain and water, heated until it thickens, then cooled and added to the dough. Like tangzhong, it gelatinizes starch so the dough holds more water, giving a softer, moister crumb that stays fresh longer. It's used in German breads and rolls, often with whole grain or rye.
shortDefinition: A cooked flour or grain paste added to dough.

definition: The main acid made by the bacteria in a sourdough starter. It has a mild, creamy, yogurt-like sourness. Warmer, wetter fermentation tends to favor lactic acid, which is why a liquid starter kept on the warm side usually tastes milder and rounder than a stiff one kept cool.
shortDefinition: The mild, yogurt-like acid in sourdough.
henrysTips: If your family says your sourdough's too sour, keep the starter and dough warmer and a little wetter. You'll tilt things toward the softer lactic side.
alternateQuestions: how to make sourdough less sour
youtubeQuery: lactic vs acetic acid sourdough flavor

definition: The bacteria in a sourdough starter that turn sugars from flour into lactic acid and, in many species, acetic acid too. They usually outnumber the wild yeast by a wide margin and are responsible for sourdough's tang, its lower pH, and much of its keeping quality. Their acids also affect gluten and help control enzyme activity, which matters a lot in rye breads.
shortDefinition: The bacteria that make sourdough sour.
henrysTips: Think of your starter as a partnership. The yeast does the lifting, the bacteria do the flavor. How you feed and where you keep it decides which partner gets the upper hand.
youtubeQuery: sourdough starter bacteria and yeast explained

definition: A curved or straight blade used to score bread before baking. Professional lames typically use a double-edged razor blade attached to a handle, allowing for clean, precise cuts.
shortDefinition: A blade tool for scoring bread.
henrysTips: Hold it at a shallow angle (about 30°) for that dramatic ear. Straight down cuts give you a different look.

definition: Dough built in many thin layers by wrapping a block of butter in dough, rolling it out, and folding it again and again. Each roll and fold is called a turn, either a single (letter) turn or a double (book) turn. In the oven, water in the butter turns to steam and pushes the layers apart, which is how croissants, puff pastry, and Danish get their flaky structure. This is a different thing from the sourdough lamination where you stretch dough thin on the counter to build strength.
shortDefinition: Butter-layered dough rolled and folded in turns.
henrysTips: The butter and the dough need to be about the same firmness. Butter that's too cold shatters, butter that's too warm smears in, and either way you lose your layers.
When the dough fights you, wrap it and chill it. Rest is part of the method.

definition: A technique where dough is stretched out very thinly on a counter (like a bedsheet) and then folded back up. It helps build gluten strength and is a great way to layer in ingredients like cheese or nuts. In pastry, 'lamination' means something different: folding a butter block into dough for croissants (see Laminated Dough).

A locally adapted grain population that farmers have selected and replanted in one region over many generations, rather than a uniform variety bred by a plant breeder. A landrace field holds a lot of genetic variety, which helps it handle local weather, pests, and soil. In the bakery that variety shows up as flour that can act a little differently from season to season, with flavor that tends to reflect where it was grown.
shortDefinition: Locally adapted, genetically varied grain kept by farmers.

definition: Porous volcanic rocks placed in a tray at the bottom of a home oven. Bakers pour boiling water over them to generate massive clouds of steam for baking hearth loaves without a Dutch oven.

A decorative pattern where shallow cuts are made to resemble the veins of a leaf. Unlike deep functional scores, these are often shallow 'artistic' scores that don't open up fully but leave a beautiful tattoo-like design.
A dough consisting primarily of flour, water, salt, and yeast, with little to no added fat or sugar. Baguettes, sourdough boules, and pizza dough are classic lean doughs.

A fold where you stretch the dough into a rough rectangle and fold it in thirds, like a business letter going into an envelope: one third over the middle, then the other third over that. Bakers use it as a strength-building fold during bulk fermentation, as part of shaping, and it's also the basic single turn in laminated doughs like croissant.
shortDefinition: Folding dough in thirds, like a business letter.
henrysTips: Stretch gently until you feel resistance, then stop. If the dough starts to tear, it's telling you it needs more rest before the next fold.

definition: A portion of active sourdough starter that has been specially prepared for baking, usually built up by feeding your starter at a specific ratio and timing. Some bakers use 'levain' and 'starter' interchangeably, but technically a levain is made from your starter.
shortDefinition: A prepared portion of starter for baking.
henrysTips: For most home bakers, you can use your fed starter directly. A separate levain is for fine-tuning timing and flavor.

definition: A stiff Italian sourdough starter (maintained at 50% hydration or less), often kept submerged in water or bound in cloth. Italian bakers rely on it to raise heavy, enriched doughs like Panettone and Colomba, and frequent feedings keep its acidity mild so it doesn't weaken those rich doughs.
A strong alkali used to dip pretzels and bagels. It creates a much darker, shinier, and more authentic crust than baking soda, but requires careful safety handling (gloves/goggles).
henrysTips: It sounds scary, but if you want 'real' pretzels, you have to use lye. Just wear gloves and don't splash!

definition: A chemical reaction between amino acids and reducing sugars that gives browned food (like bread crust) its distinctive flavor and golden color.
shortDefinition: The chemical reaction that creates the brown, tasty crust.

definition: Maltose is a sugar made of two glucose units, and in bread it's mostly produced inside the dough when amylase enzymes break down starch. Yeast and many sourdough bacteria feed on it, so a steady supply of maltose helps keep fermentation going through a long rise. Whatever sugar is left at bake time also helps the crust brown. That's why enzyme activity, damaged starch, and malt all affect how lively a dough is and how dark it bakes.
shortDefinition: Sugar released from starch that feeds yeast and browning.
henrysTips: If your long cold ferments come out with a pale crust, the yeast may have eaten most of the available sugar. A small pinch of diastatic malt can keep more sugar coming, but go easy with it.

definition: A Canadian hard red spring wheat bred from a Red Fife cross and released in the early 1900s. It ripened earlier than Red Fife, which suited the short Canadian prairie season, and it became a widely grown bread wheat in Canada and the northern US. Today it's grown mostly as a heritage variety with good baking strength.
shortDefinition: Canadian hard red spring wheat bred from Red Fife.

definition: A large, rustic French round loaf (often 1kg-2kg) made with a high percentage of whole wheat or rye flour. Its large size allows it to keep fresh for many days.
henrysTips: The ultimate 'village bread.' Because it's so big, the inside stays moist for nearly a week.

definition: In roller milling, the intermediate particles of endosperm left after the grain is first broken, which are sifted, purified, and ground further into flour. The term also gets used for the bran, germ, and leftover flour sold as a byproduct, often for animal feed. Bakers mostly run into it when reading about how commercial flour is made.
shortDefinition: Intermediate particles in roller milling, or a milling byproduct.

definition: A Japanese white bread known for its incredibly soft, feathery texture and milky sweetness. It almost always uses the Tangzhong method (cooked flour paste) to stay moist for days.

A name for several small-seeded grasses, like pearl, finger, and proso millet, grown for thousands of years across Africa and Asia. Millets are gluten-free and show up in flatbreads such as Indian bajra roti, porridges, and fermented drinks. In wheat bread, whole millet adds crunch as an inclusion or soaker, and millet flour is used in gluten-free blends.
shortDefinition: Small gluten-free grains used whole or as flour.
henrysTips: Toast whole millet in a dry pan before adding it to dough. It tastes nuttier and stays pleasantly crunchy.

definition: How warm flour gets as it's ground. Fast or fine milling builds friction, so fresh flour can come out noticeably warm. Some bakers worry that heat harms flavor and nutrients, and the evidence there is mixed, but the practical effect is clear: warm flour raises your dough temperature.
shortDefinition: How warm flour gets from the heat of grinding.
henrysTips: Feel your flour right out of the mill. If it's warm, let it sit spread out for a bit or use cooler water so your dough temperature stays on target.

definition: Bread wheat (Triticum aestivum) from varieties bred in the last several decades for yield, disease resistance, shorter stalks, and consistent milling and baking quality. It's what most supermarket flour is made from. Modern wheat is generally predictable: strong, elastic gluten and steady water absorption, which is why most bread recipes are written around it.
shortDefinition: Today's widely grown bread wheat from modern breeding.
alternateQuestions: Is modern wheat different from old wheat?

definition: Another name for a Sourdough Starter. It refers to the main culture that you keep alive and feed forever, from which you take small amounts to bake with.

A soft, leavened flatbread from South and Central Asia, traditionally slapped onto the hot inside wall of a tandoor, a clay oven, where it blisters and chars in minutes. It's commonly enriched with yogurt, sometimes milk, and often brushed with ghee or butter after baking. At home, a very hot cast iron skillet or a pizza steel under the broiler gets you close.
shortDefinition: Soft leavened flatbread traditionally baked in a tandoor.
henrysTips: Get the skillet smoking hot, and keep the naan covered in a towel as each one comes off. They stay soft and steamy.

definition: The pizza of Naples: a thin, soft center with a puffy, blistered rim called the cornicione. It's traditionally stretched by hand, typically made with Italian 00 flour, and baked in a very hot wood-fired oven for roughly 60 to 90 seconds. The Associazione Verace Pizza Napoletana (AVPN) sets the traditional standards for ingredients and method.
shortDefinition: Naples-style pizza with a puffy rim, baked fast and hot.
henrysTips: Most home ovens can't hit Neapolitan temperatures, so don't chase perfection. Preheat a steel as hot as your oven goes and finish under the broiler.
Push the air from the center toward the edge when you stretch, and leave the rim alone. That's where your cornicione comes from.

definition: A large, thin pizza sold by the slice, with a crust crisp enough to hold but flexible enough to fold in half. It's usually made with higher-protein flour, often with a little oil and sometimes sugar, and baked longer than Neapolitan pizza in gas deck ovens at lower heat. The longer bake gives it an even, golden crust.
shortDefinition: A large, thin, foldable pizza baked in deck ovens.
henrysTips: A cold rest in the fridge for a day or more does wonders for flavor and makes the dough easier to stretch thin.
youtubeQuery: New York style pizza at home

definition: Non-diastatic malt is malted grain, usually barley, that's been heated enough to inactivate its enzymes. Because the enzymes are gone, it won't break down starch in your dough. You use it for flavor, color, and a little sweetness, and it comes as a powder or as a thick syrup. It's the classic ingredient in bagel dough and the bagel boiling water, where it adds that malty taste and helps the crust brown.
shortDefinition: Heat-treated malt for flavor and color, no active enzymes.
henrysTips: Don't mix up the two malts. Non-diastatic is for flavor and color, so you can use more of it. Diastatic is active and goes in by the pinch, or you'll end up with a gummy loaf.

definition: A cereal grain used in bread as rolled oats, oat flour, or a soaker, where it adds moisture, softness, and a mild sweetness. Oat proteins don't form gluten, and oats are naturally gluten-free, but they're often cross-contaminated with wheat in fields and mills. Certified gluten-free oats exist, and some people with celiac disease still react to oats themselves.
shortDefinition: Cereal that adds softness; gluten-free only if certified.
henrysTips: Soak or scald rolled oats before they go into the dough. Dry oats pull water out of the dough and leave you with a stiff, dry loaf.

definition: A special strain of yeast (often labeled as 'SAF Gold') designed to survive in high-sugar doughs. Sugar pulls water out of yeast cells, which slows ordinary yeast way down, but this variety keeps working in sweet environments like brioche or panettone.
henrysTips: If your sweet dough takes forever to rise, the sugar's working against your yeast. Switch to the gold label and you'll see the difference.

definition: The rapid expansion of the dough during the first 10 minutes of baking. Yeast goes into a final frenzy before dying, and gases expand, causing the loaf to 'spring' up dramatically.
henrysTips: If your bread is flat, you missed the oven spring. Usually caused by weak starter or over-proofing.

definition: A small thermometer that sits or hangs inside the oven to show the actual temperature. Home ovens often run hotter or cooler than the dial says, and some have hot spots. Knowing the real number explains a lot of pale crusts, burnt bottoms, and loaves that bake slower than the recipe says.
shortDefinition: Shows the oven's real temperature, not the dial's.
henrysTips: Move it around to different racks and spots once. You'll learn where your oven runs hot, and that's worth knowing.

definition: Mixing dough so long or so hard that the gluten network starts to break down. The dough turns slack, sticky, and shiny, and it loses its spring. It's rare when you mix by hand, but it's a real risk with stand mixers on high speed. Long, intensive mixing also works in a lot of air, which oxidizes and bleaches the flour's natural pigments, leaving a whiter crumb with flatter flavor.
shortDefinition: Mixing so much the gluten breaks down and dough goes slack.

troubleshooting.problem: Dough was smooth, then turned sticky, shiny, and slack in the mixer
