troubleshooting.solution: That's overmixing. It's hard to recover, so bake it into something flat like focaccia, and next time stop as soon as the dough passes the windowpane test.

troubleshooting.problem: Crumb looks pale and the bread tastes flat
troubleshooting.solution: Shorten the mix and use lower speeds. Let folds during bulk fermentation do some of the strength-building instead.

troubleshooting.problem: Dough comes out of the mixer very warm
troubleshooting.solution: Mixer friction adds heat. Use cooler water and check dough temperature, since warm dough tears more easily and ferments faster.

henrysTips: Stay with your mixer. Stop every couple of minutes and feel the dough, because it can go from just right to too far faster than you'd think.

definition: When dough has fermented too long, the gluten network breaks down and can no longer hold gas. The dough becomes weak, sticky, and spreads out instead of rising. Overproofed bread is typically flat and dense.
shortDefinition: Dough that fermented too long and lost structure.
henrysTips: If you poke the dough and the indent doesn't spring back at all, you've gone too far. Better to underproof than overproof!

troubleshooting.problem: Dough is very flat and sticky after proofing
troubleshooting.solution: It's overproofed. Next time, reduce bulk fermentation or final proof time by 30-60 minutes.

definition: A starter that's gone past peak and run low on food. It has usually fallen back down in the jar, smells sharply sour or like acetone, and may be thin, soupy, or topped with a layer of hooch. It can still raise bread but often more slowly, and its extra acid can weaken the dough.
shortDefinition: A starter past its peak, collapsed and very sour.
henrysTips: An overripe starter isn't dead, it's hungry. Give it one or two regular feedings and it'll usually bounce right back.
alternateQuestions: starter smells like nail polish remover

definition: P/L is the second key number from the Chopin alveograph, and you'll often see it next to W on Italian and European flour bags. P is tenacity, how hard the dough resists being blown out, and L is extensibility, how far it stretches before it bursts. A high P/L means a tight, springy dough that fights shaping, and a low P/L means a slack, very stretchy dough. Bread and pizza flours are usually chosen to land in a roughly balanced middle range.
shortDefinition: Alveograph balance between dough resistance and stretch.
henrysTips: Two flours can have the same W and still feel completely different under your hands. If one keeps snapping back when you stretch a pizza, it probably has a higher P/L.

definition: French country bread, usually a large round or oval loaf with a thick crust. It's traditionally leavened with levain, and it's made mostly with white flour plus some whole wheat or rye, which gives it a little more flavor and a slightly darker crumb than a plain white loaf. A loaf like this was meant to keep for days on a farmhouse table.
shortDefinition: French country bread, often levain-leavened with some rye.
henrysTips: A small amount of rye goes a long way here. It deepens the flavor and helps the loaf stay moist for days.

definition: Also known as a 'Pullman loaf,' this is a soft, white sandwich bread baked in a rectangular pan with a sliding lid. The lid traps the dough, forcing it to fill the corners for a perfectly square slice with very little crust.

A crust that comes out light and dull instead of deep golden brown. Browning comes from the Maillard reaction and caramelization, and both need heat, time, and sugars at the surface. A pale loaf usually means the bake was too short or the oven too cool, or the dough fermented so long that the yeast and bacteria ate most of the sugars that would have browned.
shortDefinition: A crust that stays light and dull instead of browning.

troubleshooting.problem: Crust is pale even though the bake time matched the recipe
troubleshooting.solution: Check your oven with an oven thermometer. Many home ovens run cooler than the dial says. Bake longer, until the crust is deeply colored.

troubleshooting.problem: Pale crust and a sour, slack loaf
troubleshooting.solution: Likely overfermented, so there's little sugar left to brown. Shorten bulk or the final proof.

troubleshooting.problem: Pale top with a Dutch oven
troubleshooting.solution: Take the lid off for the last part of the bake so the steam escapes and the crust can color.

henrysTips: Bake it darker than you think. Most of the flavor in a crust is in the color, and a well-browned loaf tastes like bread should.
youtubeQuery: why is my bread crust pale

definition: When a loaf spreads out flat on the peel or in the oven instead of rising up. It's frustrating because the dough often looked fine in the banneton. Common causes are overproofed or overfermented dough, gluten that wasn't developed enough, more water than the flour can handle, and shaping without enough surface tension.
shortDefinition: A loaf that spreads flat instead of rising up.

troubleshooting.problem: Dough spreads as soon as it's turned out of the banneton
troubleshooting.solution: Often overproofed. Shorten the final proof, proof cooler, or try a cold proof in the fridge so the dough is firmer when it goes in.

troubleshooting.problem: Dough feels slack and weak all through bulk
troubleshooting.solution: Build more strength with extra folds, or lower the water a little until you're used to that flour.

troubleshooting.problem: Loaf holds in the banneton but slumps in the oven
troubleshooting.solution: Shape with more tension, and get it into a hot Dutch oven or onto a preheated stone or steel quickly.

henrysTips: When a new flour pancakes on you, cut the water back a bit first. Every flour drinks differently, and you can always add water next time.
youtubeQuery: why is my sourdough flat pancaking

definition: A tall, cylindrical Italian sweet bread traditionally eaten at Christmas. It is notorious for being the 'Mount Everest' of baking due to its complex multi-day sourdough process and the need to hang it upside down while cooling.
henrysTips: This is the final boss of bread baking. Don't attempt this until you're comfortable with basic sourdough!

definition: Partly baking bread, rolls, or pizza crusts until the structure sets but the crust is still pale, then cooling them and finishing the bake later. It lets you bake ahead, freeze, and serve fresh-tasting bread with a short final bake. Bakeries use it a lot, and it works well at home for holiday rolls and pizza nights.
shortDefinition: Partly baking bread now to finish baking later.
henrysTips: Bake until the inside is set but the crust has barely any color. Cool it completely on a rack before you wrap and freeze it, or trapped steam turns the crust soggy.
youtubeQuery: par baking bread rolls to freeze

definition: How fine or coarse the pieces in a flour are, also called granulation. Finer flour takes up water faster and usually makes a smoother, stronger dough, while coarser flour gives more texture but can need longer hydration and rises less. With fresh-milled flour, grind setting is one of the biggest things you control.
shortDefinition: How fine or coarse a flour is ground.
henrysTips: Rub a pinch of flour between your fingers. If it feels gritty like sand, give the dough a longer rest before you judge how much water it needs.

definition: French for 'fermented dough,' this is simply a piece of fully mixed dough saved from a previous batch. It contains flour, water, yeast, and salt, and is added to a new batch to jump-start fermentation and add flavor.
shortDefinition: Old dough saved from a previous batch to flavor the next one.
henrysTips: This is the old-school baker's secret! Save a fist-sized ball of dough from your pizza night and throw it into your next loaf for instant flavor depth.

definition: Patent flour is the most refined white flour a mill produces, taken from the streams closest to the center of the endosperm. It has the least bran and germ, so it's the whitest flour with the lowest ash and a clean, mild flavor. Millers grade it further into longer or shorter patents depending on how much of the flour they include. Many premium bread and all-purpose flours are patent flours.
shortDefinition: The whitest, most refined flour from the endosperm's center.
henrysTips: If you see 'patent' on a bag, it's telling you that flour came from the cleanest, whitest part of the kernel. It's great for a bright, open crumb, but you'll get more flavor by blending in some whole grain.

definition: The point when a fed starter or levain has risen as high as it's going to go, just before it starts to fall. At peak the top is usually domed or just beginning to flatten, the inside is full of bubbles, and the yeast is at its most active. Many bakers use their starter at or just before peak for the strongest rise.
shortDefinition: When a fed starter reaches its highest rise.
henrysTips: Put a rubber band on the jar at the starter's level right after feeding. It's the easiest way to see how high it climbed and when it started dropping back.
youtubeQuery: how to tell when sourdough starter is at peak

definition: Pentosans, also called arabinoxylans, are fiber-like carbohydrates found in the cell walls of grains. They can hold many times their own weight in water, forming a sticky, gel-like mass. In rye they do much of the work gluten does in wheat, giving rye dough its paste-like feel and helping hold the loaf together. Wheat has them too, more so in whole grain flour, and they're part of why whole wheat and rye doughs need more water.
shortDefinition: Water-loving grain carbs that give rye its structure.
henrysTips: Rye dough feels like clay, not like wheat dough, and that's the pentosans at work. Don't try to knead it into a smooth ball. Mix it well, wet your hands, and shape it gently.

definition: A scale that measures how acidic something is. Lower numbers mean more acidic, and each whole step is about ten times stronger. Sourdough bread commonly lands somewhere around pH 3.8 to 4.5, while a ripe starter usually reads lower than the finished bread. pH tells you how intense the acidity is at that moment, not the total amount of acid present.
shortDefinition: A measure of how acidic a starter or dough is.
henrysTips: You don't need a pH meter to bake great sourdough. Your nose and the starter's rise tell you most of what you need. A meter's a fun tool once you want to track consistency.

definition: A round flatbread baked across the Middle East and Eastern Mediterranean for a very long time. The pocket forms when thin dough hits a very hot oven or surface: water in the dough turns to steam and puffs the top and bottom apart. Not every regional pita has a pocket, but for the pocket kind, high heat and even thickness matter most.
shortDefinition: Round flatbread that puffs into a pocket in a hot oven.
henrysTips: Roll it evenly with no thin spots. A thin spot lets the steam escape, and you'll get a flatbread instead of a pocket.

definition: Individual portions of pizza dough that have been divided, shaped into tight balls, and allowed to rest before being stretched into pizza. This final rest allows the gluten to relax for easier stretching.
shortDefinition: Portioned and shaped pizza dough ready for stretching.
henrysTips: Don't skip the rest period after balling! If you try to stretch them immediately, they'll shrink right back.
youtubeQuery: how to shape pizza dough balls

definition: A large, flat shovel-like tool used to transfer pizza or bread into and out of a hot oven. Can be made of wood (for launching) or metal (for turning).
shortDefinition: Flat paddle for moving pizza in and out of oven.
henrysTips: Dust your peel with semolina or cornmeal, not flour. It acts like ball bearings and helps the pizza slide off smoothly.

definition: A thick slab of ceramic (stone) or steel placed in the oven to provide intense bottom heat for pizza and bread. Preheat it for at least 45 minutes at maximum temperature.
shortDefinition: Hot surface for crispy pizza and bread crusts.
henrysTips: Steel beats stone for pizza. It conducts heat roughly 18 times faster, which gives you a crispier bottom.

definition: A tactile test to check if dough is properly proofed. Press a floured finger about 1/2 inch into the dough. If it springs back slowly and leaves a slight indent, it's ready. If it springs back quickly, it needs more time. If it doesn't spring back, it's overproofed.
shortDefinition: Press dough to check if it's ready to bake.
henrysTips: This is more reliable than watching the clock. Dough doesn't wear a watch!

definition: A wet preferment made with equal parts flour and water by weight (100% hydration) and a tiny amount of yeast. It ferments for 12-16 hours and adds flavor and structure to the final dough.
shortDefinition: A liquid preferment made with flour, water, and yeast.
henrysTips: Use only a tiny pinch of yeast, like 1/8 teaspoon for 300g flour. Too much and it'll bubble over.

definition: An intermediate round of shaping performed after bulk fermentation but before the final shape. It organizes the gluten and creates a uniform surface, setting the stage for a tight final loaf.
henrysTips: Think of this like a dress rehearsal for the final shape. It doesn't have to be perfect, just get it into a round ball.

definition: A portion of the recipe's flour, water, and yeast or starter that's mixed and fermented ahead of time, then added to the final dough. Preferments bring more flavor, better keeping quality, and often better structure than mixing everything at once. The common types are poolish (wet), biga (stiff), sponge, pâte fermentée (a piece of old dough), and levain (the sourdough version).
shortDefinition: Dough made ahead and fermented to add flavor and strength.
henrysTips: If you're not ready for sourdough, a poolish made the night before is the quickest way to get that deeper, bakery-style flavor in a yeasted loaf.

definition: A thermometer with a metal needle used to check the internal temperature of the loaf. It is the only accurate way to know if bread is fully baked (usually 190°F-210°F) without cutting it open.
henrysTips: Stop thumping the bottom of the bread! Just stick a thermometer in it. 205°F means it's done. No guessing.

definition: The final rise of shaped bread dough before baking, also called 'final proof.' This can be done at room temperature (warm proof) or in the refrigerator (cold proof/retard).
shortDefinition: The final rise after shaping, before baking.
henrysTips: Cold proofing overnight in the fridge gives better flavor and makes scoring easier.

definition: A temperature-controlled box that keeps your dough at the perfect warm temperature for fermentation. It is especially useful in winter when a cold kitchen can stall your starter.
An enzyme that breaks down protein (gluten). Over time, it softens the dough. If fermentation goes on too long, protease can destroy the gluten network, leading to a sticky, runny mess.

Protein content is the share of a flour's weight that's protein, and in wheat flour most of that protein forms gluten when you add water. Higher protein usually means a flour can absorb more water and build a stronger dough, so it's a useful clue when you're choosing flour. It's not a guarantee, though: gluten quality matters just as much, and two flours with the same number can bake very differently. On US bags, protein is listed in grams per serving and rounded, so it's only a rough guide.
shortDefinition: How much protein a flour has, a clue to its strength.
henrysTips: To get a rough percentage from a US label, divide the protein grams by the serving size in grams. A 30 gram serving showing 4 grams is somewhere around 13 percent, but rounding means it could be a bit higher or lower.
alternateQuestions: how much protein in bread flour

definition: A seed that's cooked and milled like a grain but doesn't come from a grass. Buckwheat, quinoa, and amaranth are the best-known examples. True cereals like wheat, rye, oats, rice, and corn are all grasses. Pseudocereals are gluten-free (barring cross-contamination), so in bread they add flavor and nutrition but need wheat or a gluten-free binder for structure.
shortDefinition: Grain-like seed from a plant that isn't a grass.

definition: A specialized loaf pan with a slide-on lid. It is used to bake Pain de Mie (sandwich bread) so the loaf comes out with a perfectly square cross-section.

A dark, dense rye bread from Westphalia in Germany. Traditional Westphalian pumpernickel is made from coarse rye meal and cracked rye, baked in covered pans at a low temperature for many hours, often 12 or more. That long, slow bake darkens it naturally and gives it a deep, slightly sweet flavor. Many American pumpernickels are a different bread, mixing rye with wheat flour and getting their color from cocoa, coffee, or molasses.
shortDefinition: Dark, dense German rye bread baked long and slow.
henrysTips: Slice it thin and give it time. A real pumpernickel is better a day or two after baking, once the crumb has settled.

definition: A German cold soaker: grains, seeds, or meal soaked in cool or room-temperature water before going into the dough. It softens hard bits so they don't pull water from the dough or feel gritty in the crumb. Unlike a Brühstück, it uses no hot water, so the starches aren't gelatinized.
shortDefinition: A German cold soaker for grains and seeds.

definition: A seed from the Andes of South America, where it's been a staple for thousands of years. It's a pseudocereal, related to amaranth and spinach rather than to grasses. Quinoa is gluten-free. Rinse whole quinoa to remove its natural bitter coating (saponins) unless it's sold pre-rinsed. In bread, it's usually cooked and added as a soaker or inclusion, and quinoa flour goes into gluten-free blends.
shortDefinition: Andean seed used like a grain; gluten-free.

definition: A Canadian heritage hard red wheat associated with David Fife, who grew it in Ontario in the 1840s. It became an important bread wheat in Canada and was a parent of Marquis. Bakers like it for its rich, slightly spicy flavor. Its gluten is usually softer and more extensible than modern bread wheat, and it works well in whole grain and blended sourdough loaves.
shortDefinition: Canadian heritage red wheat from the 1840s.
henrysTips: Red Fife is a great first heritage wheat to mill at home. Try it at about a third of your flour before going all in.

definition: The process of slowing down fermentation by placing the dough in a cold environment (usually the fridge). This allows flavor to develop over a longer period without the dough over-proofing.

The scientific name for 'staling.' It occurs when starch molecules in the bread recrystallize and harden over time. This process happens fastest at refrigerator temperatures, which is why you should never store baked bread in the fridge.
henrysTips: The fridge is the enemy of fresh bread! It actually speeds up retrogradation. Freeze it or keep it on the counter.

definition: Finely ground rice used primarily for dusting proofing baskets (bannetons). Unlike wheat flour, rice flour doesn't absorb moisture or form a paste with the dough, preventing sticking.
shortDefinition: Non-stick flour for dusting proofing baskets.
henrysTips: Buy the cheap stuff at Asian grocery stores. You don't need fancy rice flour for dusting.

definition: A starter or levain that's fermented long enough to be ready to leaven dough. It's grown noticeably, has bubbles throughout, smells pleasantly sour or yeasty, and has a domed or just-flattening top. Ripe usually means at or near peak, the sweet spot between young and overripe.
shortDefinition: A starter that's active and ready to use in dough.
henrysTips: Look, smell, and feel. A ripe starter is airy and a little stretchy when you pull a spoon through it, not runny and not tight.
youtubeQuery: signs your sourdough starter is ready to use

definition: A cylinder for rolling dough flat and even. Handled pins are easy to start with, and straight dowel or tapered French pins give you more feel for the dough. In bread baking it rolls out flatbreads like pita, laminated doughs like croissant, cinnamon roll dough, and sandwich loaf dough before rolling it up.
shortDefinition: A cylinder for rolling dough flat and even.
henrysTips: Roll from the center out and turn the dough a quarter turn often. It keeps the thickness even and tells you right away if it's sticking.
If the dough keeps shrinking back, cover it and let it rest ten minutes. The gluten relaxes and it'll roll out easily.
youtubeQuery: how to roll out bread dough rolling pin

definition: A bacterial spoilage in bread caused by Bacillus bacteria, such as B. subtilis, whose spores can survive baking. As the loaf sits, usually in warm, humid weather, they break down the crumb, which turns sticky and stringy, pulling into threads when you tear it, with a sweet, overripe-fruit smell. A ropy loaf should be thrown out. Sourdough's acidity, clean equipment, cooling bread properly, and storing it well all help prevent it.
shortDefinition: Bacterial spoilage that makes the crumb sticky and stringy.

troubleshooting.problem: Crumb is sticky and stringy and smells sweet, like overripe fruit
troubleshooting.solution: That's rope. Throw the loaf out and don't eat it. Wash bowls, boards, bread boxes, and anything else the bread touched.

troubleshooting.problem: Rope keeps showing up in summer
troubleshooting.solution: Cool loaves on a rack until fully cool, then store them so they don't sit warm and humid. Freeze what you won't eat in a day or two.

troubleshooting.problem: Rope in yeasted loaves but not in sourdough
troubleshooting.solution: Acidity slows these bacteria. Sourdough fermentation helps, and some bakers add a little vinegar to yeasted doughs in hot weather.

henrysTips: If you tear a loaf and see fine threads stretching between the pieces, don't taste it to check. Your nose will tell you, and it goes in the trash.

definition: A French heritage red wheat dating to the 1800s, now grown in small amounts by heritage grain farmers. Bakers prize it for its rich, complex flavor in whole grain and high-extraction breads. Like many heritage wheats, its gluten tends to be softer than modern bread wheat, so it often benefits from gentle handling or blending.
shortDefinition: French heritage red wheat from the 1800s.

definition: A hand-mixing method done right in the bowl, named after the French baker Gérard Rubaud. You cup your hand like a scoop, slide it under the dough, lift and stretch it, let it fall back, and keep rotating the bowl in a steady rhythm. It develops gluten in wet doughs without slapping them on the counter, and it's a handy way to work in salt or water added late in the mix.
shortDefinition: An in-bowl hand mixing method for wet doughs.
henrysTips: Wet your hand before you start and keep a steady rhythm. It's less about force and more about lifting and stretching over and over.

definition: A flavorful flour made from rye grain that contains very little gluten-forming protein. Instead of gluten, it relies on pentosans (water-loving carbohydrates) and starch for structure, resulting in a sticky dough and a dense, moist crumb.
henrysTips: Rye dough is naturally sticky, so don't try to knead it like white bread. Think of it more like molding clay than stretching a rubber band.
commonMistakes: Trying to knead rye dough until it passes the windowpane test (it never will).

definition: A core bread ingredient that seasons the loaf, tightens the gluten so the dough is easier to handle, and slows fermentation so flavor has time to develop. Lean breads typically use around 1.8% to 2.2% of the flour weight, with 2% a common starting point. Many bakers prefer fine sea salt or non-iodized salt because it dissolves easily and tastes clean, though iodized salt still makes good bread.
shortDefinition: Seasons bread, tightens gluten, and slows fermentation.
henrysTips: Weigh your salt. A teaspoon of fine salt and a teaspoon of flaky salt are very different amounts, but 10 grams is always 10 grams.
If you forget the salt, you'll know: the dough goes slack and sticky and rises fast. Work it in as soon as you notice, even after bulk has started.
alternateQuestions: can I use iodized salt in bread
youtubeQuery: role of salt in bread dough

definition: A technique where boiling water is poured over flour (often rye or coarse grains) to soften the bran and gelatinize the starches before adding it to the main dough. It creates a sweeter, softer bread.

Heating milk to just below boiling (180°F) before adding it to bread dough. This denatures a specific protein in milk (serum whey protein) that would otherwise weaken the gluten and result in a gummy, dense loaf.
henrysTips: Grandma wasn't just doing this for fun. Skip it and your milk bread can come out tighter and shorter than it should. Heat the milk, then let it cool before it goes near your yeast.

definition: Making deliberate cuts in the surface of bread dough just before baking. These cuts control where the bread expands during oven spring and create decorative patterns.
shortDefinition: Cutting patterns in dough before baking.
henrysTips: Use a swift, confident motion. Hesitation gives you ragged cuts.

definition: The line where the dough comes together after shaping. This is usually placed face-up in the banneton so it ends up on the bottom of the loaf during baking.

A coarse, golden flour made from durum wheat. It's high in protein, but its gluten is strong and not very stretchy compared to bread wheat. It's often used for dusting pizza peels or making pasta, but adds a wonderful crunch to bread crusts.
The initial stage of mixing where flour and water are combined but no gluten has developed. The dough looks lumpy, rough, and messy, but there is no dry flour left in the bowl.
henrysTips: Don't panic when it looks like a mess here. You just want to make sure there are no dry bits of flour at the bottom of the bowl.

definition: The process of forming bulk fermented dough into its final form before proofing. Good shaping creates surface tension that helps the bread rise up instead of spreading out.
shortDefinition: Forming dough into its final shape before proofing.
henrysTips: Don't manhandle it! Gentle hands preserve the bubbles you spent all day creating.

definition: A mesh tool used to aerate flour or remove bran particles from whole grain flour (a process called 'bolting'). This allows bakers to make lighter loaves while still using whole grains.

A hand-kneading method for wet, sticky doughs. You pick the dough up, slap the bottom of it onto the counter, stretch the part you're holding toward you, and fold it back over the top, then turn it and repeat. It builds gluten quickly in high-hydration dough without adding extra flour to the bench, and the dough goes from slack and sticky to smooth and springy in a few minutes.
shortDefinition: A fast hand-kneading method for wet, sticky doughs.
henrysTips: Don't flour the counter and don't fight the stickiness. Keep your hands moving and quick, and within a few minutes the dough starts letting go of the bench on its own.
If your arms get tired, rest the dough for five minutes. The gluten keeps organizing while you take a break.
youtubeQuery: slap and fold kneading wet dough

definition: Grains or seeds that have been soaked in water (or milk) before being added to the dough. Soaking prevents hard grains from stealing moisture from the dough and making the bread dry.
A knotted bread that is dipped in a lye or baking soda solution before baking. This alkaline bath gives pretzels their signature dark mahogany color and unique pretzel flavor.

Soft wheat has a kernel with a mealy, crumbly endosperm that breaks apart easily into fine flour with less damaged starch. Its flour usually absorbs less water and tends to be lower in protein, which makes it a natural fit for cakes, cookies, biscuits, pie crust, and crackers where you want tenderness instead of chew. You can bake bread with it, but on its own it often gives a slacker dough and a lower loaf.
shortDefinition: Wheat with a crumbly kernel, usually lower in protein.
henrysTips: A little soft wheat blended into a bread dough can give you a more tender crumb. I'd keep it to a modest share of the flour until you see how your dough handles it.

definition: Soft white wheat is a low-protein wheat with a crumbly kernel and pale bran, grown mostly in the Pacific Northwest. It's used for cakes, cookies, crackers, flatbreads, and noodles, and it's the usual grain behind whole wheat pastry flour. It gives tender, delicate results, but it doesn't have the gluten strength for a tall hearth loaf on its own.
shortDefinition: Low-protein, pale wheat for pastry and tender baking.
henrysTips: Keep a bucket of soft white berries next to your hard wheat. Fresh-milled soft white makes some of the best whole grain muffins, pancakes, and pie crust you'll ever eat.

definition: A soft white heritage wheat brought to northern Mexico and the American Southwest by Spanish missionaries in the 1600s and 1700s. It's been grown in the region for centuries and is prized for flour tortillas, crackers, and pastry. Its gluten is soft and extensible, so it rolls out easily but makes a tender, lower-rising loaf on its own.
shortDefinition: Soft white heritage wheat of the Southwest, for tortillas.
henrysTips: Sonora makes lovely flour tortillas. For bread, I blend it with a stronger flour so the loaf holds its shape.

definition: A drought-hardy cereal grain that's been a staple across Africa and South Asia for a long time, used in flatbreads like Indian jowar roti and in porridges and fermented foods. It's gluten-free with a mild, slightly sweet flavor. In gluten-free baking, sorghum flour is a common base, usually combined with starches and a binder because it can't trap gas on its own.
shortDefinition: Hardy gluten-free cereal used for flatbreads.

definition: Bread leavened by a culture of wild yeast and lactic acid bacteria instead of commercial yeast. You keep that culture alive as a starter by feeding it flour and water, then use some of it to raise your dough. The bacteria make acids that give sourdough its tang and help it keep longer, while the yeast makes the gas that lifts the loaf. It's slower than yeasted bread, so timing depends on your starter's strength and your kitchen's temperature.
shortDefinition: Bread raised by wild yeast and bacteria instead of packaged yeast.
henrysTips: Don't let the word scare you. Sourdough is just flour, water, salt, and time. I wrote Sourdough for the Rest of Us because most bakers overthink it, and a healthy starter forgives a lot.
Watch the dough, not the clock. A sourdough recipe's times are a guide; your kitchen's temperature decides how fast things really move.

definition: The portion of sourdough starter that is removed before feeding to keep the total volume manageable. While not active enough to rise bread, it is packed with flavor and can be used in pancakes, crackers, and cookies.
henrysTips: Never throw this away! Keep a 'discard jar' in your fridge and make pancakes on the weekend. It's free flavor.
shortDefinition: Starter removed before feeding, great for recipes.

definition: A living culture of wild yeast and beneficial bacteria (primarily lactic acid bacteria) that naturally occurs in flour and the environment. It's maintained by regular feeding with flour and water and used to leaven bread instead of commercial yeast.
shortDefinition: Living culture of wild yeast and bacteria for leavening.
henrysTips: Name it! You're more likely to feed something called 'Herman' than 'that jar in the back of the fridge.'
bookRef: Sourdough for the Rest of Us

definition: An ancient hulled wheat (Triticum spelta) with a nutty, sweet flavor. It has highly extensible (stretchy) gluten that is weaker than modern wheat, meaning it can easily be over-kneaded and collapse if worked too hard.
henrysTips: Spelt creates a dough that spreads out like a puddle if you aren't careful. Treat it gently and use a loaf pan if you're just starting out.

definition: A mixer where the bowl turns and a spiral-shaped hook turns too, so the dough is constantly being worked against the hook. It's gentle and efficient for bread dough, builds gluten without a lot of heat, and handles large or stiff batches well. That's why spiral mixers are the standard in most bread bakeries.
shortDefinition: A mixer that turns both bowl and hook, built for bread.
henrysTips: Even with a spiral, keep an eye on dough temperature. Less heat from friction doesn't mean none.

definition: A wet pre-ferment, similar to a poolish but often containing all the liquid for the recipe. It is whipped up to incorporate air and allowed to ferment until bubbly/foamy before the remaining ingredients are added.

Sprout damage happens when wheat or rye gets wet in the field near harvest and the kernels start to germinate before they're cut. Germination switches on enzymes, especially amylase, that start breaking down starch. Flour from sprouted grain has a low falling number and can bake into a sticky, gummy crumb with weak structure and a darker crust. This is different from sprouted flour, where sprouting is done on purpose and then stopped and dried under control.
shortDefinition: Grain that started sprouting in the field, raising enzymes.
henrysTips: If you buy berries straight from a farm after a wet harvest, bake a test loaf before you commit the whole bag. Extra acidity from a sourdough can help calm down the enzymes, especially in rye.

definition: Flour made from grain that's been allowed to start sprouting, then dried and milled. Sprouting wakes up the grain's enzymes, so the flour has higher enzyme activity and a slightly sweeter flavor. Because those enzymes break down starch faster, it's usually best used as part of a blend, and you'll want to watch fermentation closely so the crumb doesn't turn gummy.
shortDefinition: Flour milled from grain that was sprouted and then dried.
henrysTips: I treat sprouted flour like a flavor booster, not the whole show. A smaller share in the blend gives you the sweetness without a sticky crumb.

definition: A countertop mixer with a bowl that stays put while a dough hook spins and moves around it. It's great for enriched doughs like brioche that need a long mix, and it saves your arms on big batches. Many home stand mixers struggle with stiff doughs or large loads, and the friction of mixing warms the dough, so watch both.
shortDefinition: A countertop mixer with a hook for kneading dough.
henrysTips: Stay on low to medium speed for bread dough. High speed heats the dough and works the motor harder than it needs to.
If the dough climbs the hook, stop, scrape it down, and keep going.

definition: A rye bread fault where amylase enzymes break down starch during baking, leaving a sticky, gummy, or cracked crumb that can pull away from the crust. Rye starch gelatinizes at temperatures where these enzymes are still active, so the enzymes get a window to break it down before the bake sets the crumb. Acidity from a rye sourdough slows that enzyme activity, which is a big reason traditional rye breads are made with sourdough.
shortDefinition: Enzymes break down rye starch in the oven, leaving a gummy crumb.

troubleshooting.problem: Rye loaf is gummy or sticky inside even after cooling
troubleshooting.solution: Use enough sourdough to acidify the dough well, and let the loaf rest before slicing. Many rye breads need a full day to set.

troubleshooting.problem: Crumb cracks or separates from the crust
troubleshooting.solution: Check your acidity and baking. More ripe rye sourdough and a full bake usually help. Flour with high enzyme activity, such as sprout-damaged flour, makes this more likely.

troubleshooting.problem: Problem appeared with a new bag of rye flour
troubleshooting.solution: Enzyme levels vary between harvests and mills. Try a higher share of rye sourdough in the dough, or a different flour.

youtubeQuery: rye bread gummy crumb starch attack

definition: The container you keep your sourdough starter in. A good one has a wide mouth for stirring and feeding, straight sides so you can see the rise, and a lid that rests loosely so gas can escape. Glass lets you see the bubbles and the level, which tells you when the starter has peaked.
shortDefinition: The container your sourdough starter lives in.
henrysTips: Put a rubber band around the jar at the level right after feeding. Then you can see at a glance how far it's risen.

definition: Water vapor introduced into the oven during the first 20 minutes of baking. Steam keeps the crust soft and flexible, allowing the bread to expand fully (oven spring) before the crust hardens.

A starter kept at low hydration, often around 50% to 60% water to flour, so it's a firm dough rather than a batter. Stiff starters usually ferment more slowly, hold longer before overripening, and tend to favor a tangier, more acetic flavor. Italian lievito madre is a well-known stiff starter used for panettone and other sweet breads.
shortDefinition: A low-hydration starter kept as a firm dough.
henrysTips: A stiff starter is handy when you travel or have a busy week. It moves slower, so it gives you more time between feedings.
youtubeQuery: how to make a stiff sourdough starter

definition: A shaping technique where you pull the sides of the dough across the center in alternating pinches, crossing left over right like lacing a shoe, while working down the length of the dough. Each pull tightens the outer skin, so it's common for batards and for slack doughs that need extra help holding their shape. Once it's stitched, you roll the dough up and seal the seam.
shortDefinition: Pulling the sides across and pinching to build tension.
henrysTips: Use a light touch and a little flour on top only. You want the dough to grip the counter underneath so you've got something to pull against.

definition: A mill that grinds grain between two stones, one turning against the other, which is the oldest form of milling. Home stone and burr mills work the same way, using stone or other grinding plates, and the gap between them can be adjusted from cracked grain to fine flour. They're usually slower than impact mills but give you more control over texture, and many bakers like the character of stone-ground flour.
shortDefinition: A mill that grinds grain between two stones or burrs.
henrysTips: If you want cracked grain for a soaker and flour for the loaf from the same machine, a stone or burr mill makes that easy because you can open the gap up.

definition: Straight grade flour is white flour made by combining all the usable flour streams from the mill, both patent and clear, instead of separating them. It has a little more ash, color, and flavor than patent flour, but it's still a refined white flour with the bran and germ removed. It's a common base for bakery flours.
shortDefinition: White flour combining all of the mill's flour streams.

definition: A gentle folding technique performed during bulk fermentation. Wet your hands, grab one side of the dough, stretch it up, and fold it over onto itself. Rotate the bowl 90° and repeat 4 times. This builds gluten strength without kneading.
shortDefinition: Folding technique to build dough strength during bulk.
henrysTips: Wet hands are your friend! Sticky dough won't stick to wet hands.

definition: The tight outer skin you build on a loaf during pre-shaping and shaping. That skin helps the dough hold its shape, push upward in the oven instead of spreading, and open cleanly where you score it. Too little and the loaf slumps; too much and the surface tears.
shortDefinition: The tight outer skin built on dough during shaping.
henrysTips: Look for a smooth, taut surface that springs back slowly when you touch it. If you see the skin starting to tear, you've gone far enough.

definition: An Asian technique where a small portion of flour is cooked with water to create a gel-like paste, then added to the dough. The gelatinized starches hold extra moisture, making bread incredibly soft and extending shelf life.
shortDefinition: Cooked flour paste that makes bread super soft.
henrysTips: This is the secret to that pillowy-soft Japanese milk bread. It makes a real difference in sandwich loaves.

definition: A tiny grain from Ethiopia and Eritrea, where it's been grown for thousands of years and is the traditional grain behind injera, the spongy, sour fermented flatbread at the center of many meals. Teff is gluten-free and comes in ivory and brown types. Its seeds are so small that the whole grain is milled into flour, bran and all.
shortDefinition: Tiny Ethiopian and Eritrean grain behind injera.
youtubeQuery: how to make injera with teff

definition: Adding a measured amount of water to grain and letting it rest before milling. It's standard in commercial milling because it toughens the bran so it comes off in bigger flakes and softens the endosperm so it grinds cleanly. Many home millers skip it, while some lightly temper grain they plan to sift to make the bran easier to separate.
shortDefinition: Moistening and resting grain before milling.
henrysTips: Check your mill's instructions before tempering. Damp grain can gum up some mills, especially impact mills.

definition: A technical term for dough that resists stretching entirely. A 'bucky' or tenacious dough feels tough and rubbery, often caused by using flour with too much protein or over-kneading.

A shaping motion where the baker drags the dough ball across the counter surface towards themselves. The friction against the counter tightens the outer skin of the dough, helping it stand tall in the oven.
youtubeQuery: how to create tension in bread dough

definition: A French word for the way place shapes flavor: soil, climate, weather, and farming practices. It's borrowed from wine, and bakers use it for grain too, since the same wheat variety can taste and perform differently depending on where and in what year it was grown. You'll notice it most with fresh-milled, whole grain, and identity-preserved flours.
shortDefinition: How growing place and season shape a grain's flavor.
henrysTips: If you want to taste terroir, bake the same simple recipe with two whole wheat flours from different farms side by side. Keep everything else the same.

definition: A lab measure of the total amount of acid in a starter or dough, found by neutralizing a sample with a base solution to a set endpoint. pH shows how intense the acidity is, while titratable acidity shows how much acid there is in all, and the two don't always move together. It's mostly a tool for labs, mills, and advanced bakers studying flavor and consistency.
shortDefinition: Total acid in a dough, as opposed to pH intensity.

definition: A grain bred by crossing wheat with rye. It carries traits of both: some wheat gluten, plus rye-like flavor and a tendency toward high enzyme activity. Triticale flour on its own makes a dense, slightly sticky loaf, so bakers usually blend it with wheat flour.
shortDefinition: Wheat and rye cross with traits of both.
henrysTips: Treat triticale a bit like a light rye. Watch the fermentation closely and don't let it run long.

definition: A troubleshooting term for large, unwanted caverns or holes in the crumb, often right under the crust, while the rest of the crumb is dense. Common causes include underproofing, uneven shaping that traps air pockets, and pockets of flour rolled into the dough.

troubleshooting.problem: Large tunnel at the top of the loaf
troubleshooting.solution: Often underproofing or weak structure. Let the dough ferment longer.

troubleshooting.problem: Random caverns through the loaf
troubleshooting.solution: Degas gently during pre-shape, brush excess flour off the dough before shaping, and seal seams well.

definition: A heritage hard red winter wheat brought to Kansas by Mennonite immigrants in the 1870s. It helped make the Great Plains a major wheat-growing region. Today it's grown in small amounts for heritage flour, and bakers value its deep wheat flavor, though its gluten is usually less predictable than modern hard red winter wheat.
shortDefinition: Heritage hard red winter wheat brought to Kansas, 1870s.

definition: A small, round, metal pizza peel used specifically to rotate the pizza inside a wood-fired oven. Unlike the launching peel, it is designed for agility inside the hot oven.

Type 00 is the most refined Italian flour grade: very finely milled, white, and low in ash. The grade only describes refinement, not strength, so protein varies a lot. A 00 made for pizza can be quite strong, while a 00 made for pastry or fresh pasta can be soft and weak. It's not automatically pizza flour, so check the protein or W on the bag before you use it.
shortDefinition: Finely milled, low-ash Italian flour; strength varies.
henrysTips: Pizza 00 flours are usually built for very hot ovens. In a home oven that tops out lower, they can bake up pale, so many bakers mix in some bread flour or add a little malt or sugar for color.

definition: In much of Europe, flour is labeled by type based on ash content, the mineral left after burning a sample, which shows how much of the outer kernel ended up in the flour. French types are based on ash, with T55 at roughly 0.50 to 0.60 percent ash and then T65, T80, T110, and T150 for whole wheat. German types list approximate ash in milligrams per 100 grams, so 405, 550, 1050, and 1600 for wheat, and rye has its own set of types. Italian grades 00, 0, 1, 2, and integrale describe how refined the flour is, which mostly tracks ash too. These numbers are approximate, and none of them tell you protein or strength.
shortDefinition: European flour grades based mainly on ash content.
henrysTips: A higher type number means more of the outer kernel, so more color, more flavor, and usually more thirst. It doesn't mean stronger, so check the protein or W if a recipe needs a strong flour.
T65 is a lovely flour for country bread. If you can't get it, a mix of bread flour with a small share of whole wheat gets you in the neighborhood.

definition: Dough that didn't ferment long enough during bulk, so it hasn't built enough gas, acidity, or flavor before shaping. Underfermented bread is often dense and tight, with a gummy texture and sometimes big irregular holes under a tight crumb, sometimes called fool's crumb. It's different from underproofed: underfermented is about bulk not going far enough, while underproofed is about the final proof after shaping.
shortDefinition: Dough that didn't ferment long enough in bulk.

troubleshooting.problem: Dense, tight crumb with a few large holes near the top
troubleshooting.solution: Lengthen bulk fermentation until the dough is domed, jiggly, and bubbly at the sides. An aliquot jar helps you see the real rise.

troubleshooting.problem: Bulk seems to take forever and the dough barely moves
troubleshooting.solution: Check your dough temperature. A cold dough ferments slowly, so aim for a warmer spot or warmer water, and make sure your starter was at peak when you mixed.

troubleshooting.problem: Loaf tastes flat and the crumb is gummy
troubleshooting.solution: Give bulk more time before shaping, and bake fully. Underfermented dough often bakes up both bland and gummy.

henrysTips: Most bakers who think they have a shaping problem actually have a fermentation problem. Go longer in bulk before you blame your hands.

definition: When dough hasn't fermented long enough. The yeast hasn't produced enough gas, resulting in dense bread with poor oven spring. When you do the poke test, the dough springs back very quickly.
shortDefinition: Dough that needs more time to rise.
henrysTips: Underproofing is better than overproofing. You can always give it 30 more minutes, but you can't undo overproofing.

troubleshooting.problem: Bread is dense with small holes
troubleshooting.solution: Likely underproofed. Give it more time during bulk fermentation or final proof.

definition: A powdered form of almost pure gluten. It is used as an additive to boost the strength of weak flours, like all-purpose or whole wheat, effectively turning them into 'bread flour'.
henrysTips: A tablespoon of this can save a loaf if you're forced to bake with cheap all-purpose flour.

definition: A German whole-grain bread, usually mostly rye, that's dense, moist, and baked in a loaf pan. It's often packed with soaked cracked grains and seeds like sunflower, and it's usually leavened with rye sourdough, since rye needs that acidity to bake up properly. The dough is more like a thick paste than a dough you shape.
shortDefinition: Dense German whole-grain rye bread baked in a pan.
henrysTips: Wrap it and wait a day before slicing. Many bakers do, because the crumb is sticky until it's had time to set.

definition: W is a measure of flour strength from the Chopin alveograph, a lab test that blows a thin sheet of dough into a bubble until it bursts. W reflects the work needed to inflate that bubble, so a higher W means a stronger flour. It's printed on many Italian and European flour bags. As a rough guide, lower W flours suit quick doughs, crackers, and pastry, middle values suit everyday bread and pizza, and higher W flours are built for long fermentation and heavy enriched doughs like panettone.
shortDefinition: Alveograph number for flour strength, common on Italian bags.
henrysTips: If an Italian pizza or panettone recipe calls for a certain W, try to stay close to it. A flour that's much weaker than the recipe expects can tear or collapse partway through a long ferment.

definition: The whole wheat kernel with only the inedible hull removed, containing the bran, germ, and endosperm. It's what home millers buy and grind into flour, and it can also be cooked, cracked, or sprouted. Whole berries keep much longer than flour when stored cool and dry.
shortDefinition: The whole wheat kernel: bran, germ, and endosperm.
henrysTips: I keep my berries in sealed buckets in a cool spot. Bought in bulk, they're the cheapest good flour you'll ever use.

definition: Wheat in the US is sorted into classes by kernel hardness, bran color, and growing season. Winter wheat is planted in fall and harvested the next summer, while spring wheat is planted in spring where winters are too harsh and harvested later that summer. The main US classes are hard red winter, hard red spring, hard white, soft red winter, soft white, and durum. Hardness is about kernel texture, not protein, though hard wheats tend to run higher in protein and that's why they're used for bread.
shortDefinition: How wheat is grouped by hardness, color, and season.
henrysTips: When you buy berries for home milling, the class tells you more than the brand name does. Hard for bread, soft for pastry, and red or white comes down to flavor and color.

definition: A classic decorative scoring pattern that resembles a stalk of wheat. It is created by making small, alternating diagonal snips or cuts down the center of the loaf.

Flour milled from the entire wheat kernel, including the bran, germ, and endosperm. Because it contains the sharp bran and oily germ, it absorbs more water and ferments faster than white flour, often producing a denser but more flavorful loaf.
henrysTips: Whole wheat is 'thirsty'! You'll almost always need to add a splash more water than the recipe calls for if you're swapping this in.

troubleshooting.problem: Loaf is dense and heavy
troubleshooting.solution: Increase hydration or mix with 50% bread flour to lighten the texture.

definition: A technique to check if gluten is fully developed. You gently stretch a small piece of dough between your fingers; if it stretches thin enough to let light through without tearing (like a windowpane), the gluten is ready.
henrysTips: Don't skip this! If the dough tears instantly, keep mixing. If you bake before this stage, your bread will be dense.
youtubeQuery: how to do windowpane test bread

definition: A single-celled fungus that eats sugars in dough and gives off carbon dioxide and alcohol, which raise the bread and build flavor. Commercial yeast is one carefully selected strain, Saccharomyces cerevisiae, grown for fast, predictable rising and sold as fresh, active dry, instant, or osmotolerant yeast. Wild yeast lives in a sourdough starter alongside lactic acid bacteria and usually works more slowly. When a recipe says "yeasted," it usually means commercial yeast rather than sourdough.
shortDefinition: The living organism that makes bread dough rise.
henrysTips: Instant yeast is the easiest for most home bakers: it goes straight in with the flour. If you swap types, adjust the amount, because fresh, active dry, and instant aren't used gram for gram.
Salt and yeast can sit in the same bowl, just don't leave them in a concentrated pile together for long. Mix them into the flour and you're fine.
alternateQuestions: what kind of yeast should I use
youtubeQuery: types of yeast for bread baking

definition: A natural leaven made by letting fruit such as raisins, apples, or other fruit ferment in water until it's bubbly and full of wild yeast. The strained liquid can be used to build a levain or mixed straight into dough. Yeast water usually brings less sourness than a sourdough starter, so it's popular for soft, sweet, and enriched breads.
shortDefinition: A wild leaven made by fermenting fruit in water.
henrysTips: I wrote The Yeast Water Handbook because yeast water gets overlooked. Start with raisins, keep the jar somewhere warm, and give it a swirl each day. When it fizzes like soda when you open it, it's ready to work.

definition: A levain used before it reaches full peak, while it's still rising and only mildly sour. It brings less acidity to the dough, so the bread tends to taste milder and the gluten stays a bit stronger. Bakers often use a young levain for milder loaves and some enriched doughs, knowing fermentation may run a little slower.
shortDefinition: A levain used early, before peak, for milder flavor.
henrysTips: If you're baking for kids or folks who don't love tang, try mixing your dough with the levain a little early. It's one of the easiest ways to soften the sour.

definition: A Japanese method where boiling water is mixed into flour, then the mixture rests, often overnight in the fridge, before being added to the dough. The hot water gelatinizes some of the starch so the dough holds more moisture, giving soft, springy, slow-to-stale bread like Japanese milk bread. It's close to tangzhong, but the flour is scalded with boiling water instead of cooked on the stove.
shortDefinition: A Japanese scald of flour with boiling water.
henrysTips: Cover the yudane right away so it doesn't dry out on top, and let it cool fully before it goes in your dough.
